topics.t: Individual differences and the person–situation interaction
topics.h: Two batsmen face the same last over with 12 runs needed. One goes calm and finds gaps; the other freezes. Same pitch, same bowler — so what made the difference?
p: Individual differences are the distinctiveness and variations among people in their characteristics and patterns of behaviour. Psychology studies, describes and measures these variations.
People differ in physical features and in psychological attributes such as intelligence, aptitude, interest, personality and values.

Behaviour is shaped both by the person and by the situation. Situationism is the view that situations and circumstances strongly influence how we act; the modern view stresses the interaction of person and situation.
A trait is a relatively stable and enduring characteristic (for example, being punctual or friendly) that shows up across many situations.
Because traits are fairly stable, they help us predict behaviour — but strong situations (an exam hall, a funeral) can make most people behave alike.

ex.q: In a silent exam hall, both the most talkative and the quietest students in a class sit silently. What does this show about behaviour?
st: Talkativeness is a fairly stable trait, so we expect differences between the two students.
But the exam hall is a strong situation with clear rules about silence.
So the situation, not the trait, decides behaviour here.
Outside the hall, the trait difference shows up again — behaviour comes from person × situation.
ex.a: Behaviour depends on the interaction of individual traits and situational demands; strong situations can override trait differences.

topics.rl: IPL scouts look at how a player handles pressure — some young players shine in a packed stadium, others struggle. Selectors are reading individual differences in the same situation.

rv.summary: People differ in physical and psychological attributes such as intelligence, aptitude, interest, personality and values. Behaviour depends on the interaction of stable traits and the situation; strong situations can make people behave alike.
focus: What a trait is and how it predicts behaviour
Situationism and the person × situation view
Why strong situations reduce trait differences
remember: Individual differences: distinctiveness and variations among people in characteristics and behaviour
Trait: relatively stable, enduring characteristic seen across situations
Situationism: situations strongly influence behaviour
traps: Don't call a one-time feeling (nervousness before one speech) a trait
Traits do not fully decide behaviour in every situation
Behaviour is not only the situation or only the person: it is their interaction

topics.t: Assessing psychological attributes
topics.h: A school counsellor in Pune has 40 students asking 'Which stream should I choose?' Guesswork won't do — she needs a systematic way to measure abilities and interests.
p: Assessment is the measurement of psychological attributes of individuals and their evaluation, often using multiple methods, against standards of comparison. Formal assessment is objective, standardised and organised; informal assessment varies from person to person and is more open to subjectivity.

Intelligence: the global capacity to understand the world, think rationally and use available resources effectively when faced with challenges. Aptitude: the underlying potential to acquire skills with training.

Interest: a preference for engaging in one or more specific activities. Personality: relatively enduring characteristics that make a person distinct. Values: enduring beliefs about an ideal mode of behaviour.

Methods: psychological test (a standardised, objective measuring instrument), interview (conversation to gather information), case study (in-depth study of one person using many sources), observation (systematic, organised, objective recording of behaviour) and self-report (the person gives information about herself or himself).

ex.q: A counsellor wants to know (a) whether Aarav has the potential to learn coding quickly, and (b) whether he actually enjoys coding. Which attributes is she assessing?
st: Potential to acquire a skill with training = aptitude.
Preference for engaging in an activity = interest.
Both are needed: aptitude plus interest predicts success.
ex.a: (a) Aptitude, (b) Interest.

topics.rl: Before campus placements, many Indian engineering colleges run aptitude tests and interviews. Companies combine a standardised test with an interview — that is assessment using multiple methods.

rv.summary: Assessment measures and evaluates psychological attributes like intelligence, aptitude, interest, personality and values, formally or informally. Methods include psychological tests, interviews, case studies, observation and self-report.
focus: Why aptitude and interest together predict success
remember: Intelligence: global capacity to understand the world, think rationally and use resources
Aptitude: potential to acquire skills with training
Interest: preference for specific activities
Values: enduring beliefs about ideal behaviour
traps: Don't swap aptitude (potential) with interest (liking)
Casual watching is not scientific observation
High aptitude alone does not guarantee success

topics.t: What is intelligence? Binet, Spearman and Thurstone
topics.h: Is a topper who aces maths but can't find her way in a new city 'intelligent'? Psychologists have argued about this for over a century.
p: Alfred Binet saw intelligence as the ability to judge well, understand well and reason well. David Wechsler defined it as the global and aggregate capacity to think rationally, act purposefully and deal effectively with one's environment.

Psychometric approach: intelligence is an aggregate of abilities, expressed as a single index (score) and measured by tests. The information-processing approach instead studies the processes people use in intellectual reasoning.
Binet's uni-factor (one-factor) theory: intelligence is one similar set of abilities used for solving any problem.
Charles Spearman's two-factor theory: a general factor (g) common to all mental tasks, plus specific factors (s) unique to particular abilities (for example, mathematical or musical).

Louis Thurstone's primary mental abilities: verbal comprehension, numerical abilities, spatial relations, perceptual speed, word fluency, memory and inductive reasoning — seven relatively independent abilities.

ex.q: Kabir scores well on almost every school subject, but he is exceptionally good at music. Explain this using Spearman's theory.
st: Spearman: every mental task draws on a general factor g plus a specific factor s.
Good performance across all subjects suggests high g.
Exceptional music skill suggests an additional strong specific factor for music.
ex.a: Kabir has high general intelligence (g) and a strong specific (s) factor for music.

topics.rl: Government recruitment exams like SSC test reasoning, numerical ability and verbal ability as separate sections — very close to Thurstone's idea of separate primary abilities.

rv.summary: Binet saw intelligence as judging, understanding and reasoning well (one factor); Wechsler as a global capacity. Spearman proposed g plus s factors, and Thurstone seven primary mental abilities. The psychometric approach measures intelligence by tests.
remember: Spearman: g (general) + s (specific)
Thurstone's 7: verbal comprehension, numerical, spatial relations, perceptual speed, word fluency, memory, inductive reasoning
Binet: uni-factor theory
traps: Interpersonal ability is Gardner's, not one of Thurstone's abilities
's' in Spearman means specific, not social
The 180-ability model is Guilford's, not Thurstone's

topics.t: Jensen's levels and Guilford's structure-of-intellect
topics.h: Memorising the periodic table is one skill; using it to predict how sodium reacts with water is another. Jensen said these are two different levels of ability.
p: Arthur Jensen proposed a hierarchical model with two levels. Level I is associative learning, where output is similar to input (for example, rote learning and memory).
Level II is cognitive competence: higher-order skills that transform the input to produce an effective output (for example, reasoning and problem-solving).

J.P. Guilford's structure-of-intellect model classifies intellectual traits along three dimensions: operations (what the person does), contents (the nature of the material) and products (the form in which information is processed).

Guilford: 6 operations (cognition, memory recording, memory retention, divergent production, convergent production, evaluation), 5 contents (visual, auditory, symbolic, semantic, behavioural) and 6 products (units, classes, relations, systems, transformations, implications).
So the model has 6 × 5 × 6 = 180 cells, each representing a distinct intellectual ability.

ex.q: How many separate abilities does Guilford's model predict, and how?
st: Operations = 6
Contents = 5
Products = 6
Abilities = 6 × 5 × 6 = 180
ex.a: 180 abilities

topics.rl: A student cramming formulae for JEE uses Jensen's Level I; solving a new problem that combines those formulae uses Level II — that is why coaching institutes stress practice problems, not just formula sheets.

rv.summary: Jensen's model has Level I (associative learning, output like input) and Level II (cognitive competence, transforming input). Guilford's structure-of-intellect combines 6 operations, 5 contents and 6 products into 180 abilities.

Guilford's three dimensions and their parts
remember: Level I: associative learning (rote memory)
Level II: cognitive competence (reasoning)
Guilford: 6 operations × 5 contents × 6 products = 180 abilities
traps: Divergent production is an operation, not a content or product
Semantic is a content; transformations and implications are products
Jensen did not propose seven primary abilities; Thurstone did

topics.t: Gardner's multiple intelligences
topics.h: A tabla maestro, a chess grandmaster and a tribal healer who knows hundreds of forest plants — are they intelligent in the same way? Howard Gardner said: different intelligences!
p: Howard Gardner proposed that intelligence is not one entity; there are distinct, relatively independent types of intelligence that interact to find solutions.

Linguistic (using language fluently — poets, writers); logical-mathematical (logical and abstract thinking, problem-solving — scientists); spatial (forming and using mental images — pilots, sailors, sculptors, architects).
Musical (sensitivity to rhythm, pitch and sound patterns — musicians); bodily-kinaesthetic (using the whole or parts of the body with skill and flexibility — athletes, dancers, actors).

Interpersonal (understanding others' motives, feelings and behaviour — counsellors, psychologists, social activists); intrapersonal (knowing one's own feelings, motives and strengths — philosophers, spiritual leaders).
Naturalistic: sensitivity to and recognition of the features of the natural world, such as plants and animals — farmers, botanists, zoologists, bird watchers.

ex.q: Mira can identify over 200 bird species by their calls and loves cataloguing butterflies. Which intelligence does she show most?
st: Classifying and recognising plants and animals is the key feature.
That matches naturalistic intelligence.
It is not musical, even though calls are sounds — she is identifying living things.
ex.a: Naturalistic intelligence

topics.rl: Dancers in Kathak need bodily-kinaesthetic intelligence, sitar players musical intelligence, and a Kerala fisherman reading sea and sky shows naturalistic and spatial skill — Gardner's theory fits India's rich range of talents.

rv.summary: Gardner proposed eight relatively independent intelligences: linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal and naturalistic.

Matching a person or job to an intelligence

Naturalistic: recognising features of the natural world
traps: Don't mix up interpersonal (others) and intrapersonal (self)
Gardner's intelligences are relatively independent: strength in one does not imply another
Naturalistic is about nature, not about people's motives

topics.t: Sternberg's triarchic theory and the PASS model
topics.h: A chaiwala who adjusts prices for office crowds, adds a new snack before Diwali and remembers every regular's order — Sternberg would call that practical intelligence in action.
p: Robert Sternberg's triarchic theory (1985) sees intelligence as the ability to adapt, to shape and to select one's environment to achieve one's goals. It has three parts.

Componential (analytical) intelligence: analysis of information to solve problems. Its components: knowledge acquisition (learning and acquiring), meta or higher-order (planning what to do and how), and performance (actually doing it).

Experiential (creative) intelligence: using past experiences creatively to solve novel problems. Contextual (practical) intelligence: dealing with environmental demands in daily life — 'street smartness' or 'business sense'.
PASS model (J.P. Das, Jack Naglieri and John Kirby): intellectual activity depends on three functional units of the brain — Arousal/Attention, Simultaneous and Successive processing, and Planning.

Simultaneous processing grasps relations among concepts as a meaningful whole (as in Raven's Progressive Matrices); successive processing handles information in serial order (recalling digits, learning spellings). Planning sets and evaluates a course of action. Das and Naglieri built the Cognitive Assessment System (CAS) to measure these processes.

ex.q: Riya memorises a 10-digit phone number by repeating it in order. Later she looks at a pattern puzzle and sees how all the pieces relate as a whole. Classify each using PASS.
st: Recalling digits in a fixed order = successive processing.
Seeing relationships among parts as one meaningful pattern = simultaneous processing.
ex.a: Phone number: successive processing; pattern puzzle: simultaneous processing.

topics.rl: Startup founders in Bengaluru often say 'business sense beats marks'. Sternberg agrees that contextual (practical) intelligence is real intelligence, even if school tests miss it.

rv.summary: Sternberg's triarchic theory has componential, experiential and contextual intelligence. The PASS model (Das, Naglieri, Kirby) explains intelligence through arousal/attention, simultaneous and successive processing, and planning, measured by the CAS.
focus: Sternberg's three intelligences and the components of componential intelligence
remember: Componential components: knowledge acquisition, meta (planning), performance
Contextual = 'street smartness'
PASS: Planning, Arousal/Attention, Simultaneous and Successive processing
CAS by Das and Naglieri
traps: Don't confuse simultaneous (whole pattern) with successive (serial order) processing
Planning before a task is the meta component, not the performance component
Street smartness is contextual, not experiential, intelligence

topics.t: Mental age, IQ and the normal curve
topics.h: A 10-year-old solves puzzles that most 12-year-olds solve. Is she 'two years ahead'? Binet's idea of mental age turned that hunch into a number.
p: Binet and Simon built the first intelligence test (1905). Mental age (MA) is a measure of a person's intellectual functioning relative to people of the same age group; chronological age (CA) is biological age since birth.
William Stern introduced the intelligence quotient: IQ = (MA ÷ CA) × 100. When MA equals CA, IQ = 100; a bright child has MA > CA, so IQ > 100.
IQ scores in a population are normally distributed: a bell-shaped, symmetrical curve with the mean at 100. Most people score near the middle; very high and very low scores are rare.
NCERT classification: above 130 very superior; 120–130 superior; 110–119 high average; 90–109 average; 80–89 low average; 70–79 borderline; below 70 intellectually disabled.
About half the population falls in the average range (90–109). Always state units: MA and CA are in years (months can be converted, e.g. 6 months = 0.5 year).

ex.q: Neha's chronological age is 10 years and her mental age is 12 years 6 months. Find her IQ and classify it.
st: Convert MA: 12 years 6 months = 12.5 years.
125 lies in 120–130, so 'superior'.
ex.a: IQ = 125 (superior).

topics.rl: Think of IQ like a cricket strike rate: it is a ratio scaled by 100. A strike rate of 100 means a run a ball — an IQ of 100 means mental age matches chronological age.

rv.summary: Mental age measures intellectual functioning relative to one's age group. Stern's IQ = (MA ÷ CA) × 100. IQ scores follow a normal curve with mean 100, and NCERT groups them from very superior (above 130) to intellectually disabled (below 70).

Classifying an IQ score into the NCERT category

topics.t: Intellectual disability and giftedness
topics.h: At both ends of the bell curve are people who need understanding and the right support — one group to build everyday skills, the other to stay challenged and motivated.
p: Intellectual disability (American Association on Mental Retardation definition): significantly below-average general intellectual functioning, together with deficits in adaptive behaviour, appearing during the developmental period (before 18 years). An IQ below 70 alone is not enough.
Adaptive behaviour is the ability to be self-reliant and to adjust to the environment — communication, self-care, social skills, daily living.

Levels: mild (IQ about 55 to 70), moderate (35–40 to 50–55), severe (20–25 to 35–40) and profound (below 20–25). People with mild disability can often learn practical skills and hold jobs; those with moderate disability can learn self-care and simple social skills with training; severe and profound levels need constant support and care.

Giftedness is exceptional general ability shown in superior performance across many areas; talent is remarkable ability in a specific field. Lewis Terman's long-term study in the 1920s followed high-IQ children to see how intelligence related to success and adjustment.

Signs of gifted children: advanced logical thinking and problem-solving, high speed of processing, superior generalisation and discrimination, originality and creative thinking, high intrinsic motivation and self-esteem, independent and non-conformist thinking, and a liking for solitary academic work. Teachers, parents and tests together help identify them.

ex.q: A 9-year-old scores an IQ of 65 but takes care of himself, communicates well and manages daily tasks like his peers. Can he be classed as having intellectual disability?
st: The definition needs two things: below-average intellect AND deficits in adaptive behaviour.
His IQ is below 70, but his adaptive behaviour is not impaired.
So the definition is not fully met.
ex.a: No — without deficits in adaptive behaviour, a low IQ score alone does not meet the definition.

topics.rl: Programmes like special schools under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act and talent-search exams for gifted students show India trying to serve both ends of the curve.

rv.summary: Intellectual disability means significantly below-average intellect plus deficits in adaptive behaviour, appearing before 18, at mild, moderate, severe or profound levels. Giftedness is exceptional general ability; talent is ability in a specific field.

topics.t: Culture and intelligence: technological vs integral
topics.h: In some cultures the 'smartest' person finishes a task fastest. In others, the smartest is the one who keeps the family and village in harmony. Who's right?
p: Culture shapes what counts as intelligent behaviour. Sternberg's contextual intelligence implies intelligence is partly a product of culture, and Vygotsky held that cultures provide the tools for thinking.

Technological intelligence (individualistic, Western-type societies) values generalisation and abstraction, speed, minimal moves and mental manipulation — attention, observation, analysis, performance, speed and achievement orientation.
Integral intelligence (many Asian and African societies) emphasises connectivity with the social and natural environment.

The Indian notion of intelligence, buddhi (as J.P. Das describes it), includes mental effort, determined action, feelings and opinions along with cognitive competence, and knowledge of one's own self, conscience, initiative and will.

Four competencies in the Indian view: cognitive capacity (sensitivity to context, understanding, discrimination, problem-solving, effective communication); social competence (respect for social order, commitment to elders, the young and the needy, concern for others); emotional competence (self-regulation and self-monitoring of emotions, honesty, politeness, good conduct); entrepreneurial competence (commitment, persistence, patience, hard work, vigilance, goal-directed behaviour).

ex.q: Classify: (a) a person who calmly controls anger and stays polite; (b) one who keeps working on a small business despite setbacks.
st: Self-regulation of emotions and politeness = emotional competence.
Persistence, patience and goal-directed hard work = entrepreneurial competence.
ex.a: (a) Emotional competence, (b) Entrepreneurial competence.

topics.rl: A self-help group of women in rural Rajasthan running a dairy cooperative shows the Indian integral idea — social harmony, patience and persistence are as 'intelligent' as speed.

rv.summary: Culture shapes what counts as intelligence. Technological intelligence values abstraction, speed and achievement; integral intelligence values connectivity with society and nature. The Indian buddhi includes cognitive, social, emotional and entrepreneurial competence.

topics.t: Emotional intelligence
topics.h: A captain who notices a teammate's shaking hands and calms him before a super over isn't using IQ — that's EQ at work.
p: The term emotional intelligence was introduced by Peter Salovey and John Mayer and popularised by Daniel Goleman (1995). It is often expressed as EQ (emotional quotient).
Salovey and Mayer: the ability to monitor one's own and others' emotions, to discriminate among them, and to use this information to guide one's thinking and actions.

Emotionally intelligent persons perceive and are sensitive to feelings; detect emotions in self and others through body language, voice and facial expressions; relate emotions to thoughts while solving problems; understand the influence of emotions' nature and intensity; and control and regulate emotions while dealing with self and others.
In short: self-awareness, managing emotions, empathy and handling relationships.
Emotional literacy programmes in schools aim to raise emotional intelligence; they are linked to better self-esteem, fewer behaviour problems and better academic and social adjustment.

ex.q: Before a debate, Tara notices her heart racing, names the feeling 'nervousness', takes slow breaths and reminds herself she has prepared. Which EI features is she showing?
st: Noticing and naming her own emotion = self-awareness.
Using breathing and self-talk to calm down = managing/regulating emotions.
Linking the emotion to a thought ('I have prepared') = relating emotions to thinking.
ex.a: Self-awareness, emotion regulation and using emotions to guide thinking.

topics.rl: Many Indian schools now run social-emotional learning periods, such as Delhi government schools' Happiness Curriculum, which includes mindfulness and reflection — an example of an emotional literacy programme.

rv.summary: Emotional intelligence, introduced by Salovey and Mayer and popularised by Goleman, is the ability to monitor one's own and others' emotions, tell them apart and use them to guide thinking and action.
focus: Self-awareness, managing emotions, empathy and handling relationships
remember: EI introduced by Salovey and Mayer; popularised by Goleman (1995)
EI: monitor own and others' emotions, discriminate among them, use this to guide thinking and action
EQ = emotional quotient
traps: High IQ does not guarantee high EQ
Goleman popularised EI but did not introduce the term

topics.t: Aptitude: nature and measurement
topics.h: Two students love aeroplanes. One also has strong mechanical reasoning and spatial skill. Who is more likely to succeed as an aircraft engineer?
p: Aptitude is a combination of characteristics indicating a person's potential to acquire some specific knowledge or skill after training.
Aptitude and interest work together: a person with high aptitude AND interest in a field is more likely to succeed in it.

Aptitude tests come in two forms: independent (specialised) aptitude tests for one area (for example, clerical or mechanical), and multiple (generalised) aptitude test batteries measuring several aptitudes.

The Differential Aptitude Tests (DAT) have eight subtests: verbal reasoning, numerical reasoning, abstract reasoning, clerical speed and accuracy, mechanical reasoning, space relations, spelling and language usage. J.M. Ojha developed an Indian adaptation.
Uses: career guidance, educational and vocational counselling, and selection for jobs or training programmes.

ex.q: A student scores high on mechanical reasoning and space relations in the DAT but low on clerical speed. Which careers might a counsellor discuss first?
st: High mechanical reasoning + space relations → skills for engineering, design, technical trades.
Low clerical speed → routine data-entry jobs may be less suited.
Check interest too, since aptitude + interest predicts success.
ex.a: Engineering or technical fields (after confirming the student's interest).

topics.rl: Armed forces selection boards in India use aptitude batteries before training pilots; the logic is that training is costly, so it pays to find people with the potential to learn fast.

rv.summary: Aptitude is the potential to acquire specific knowledge or skill after training. It is measured by independent tests or multiple batteries like the DAT (eight subtests), and is used with interest for guidance and selection.

topics.t: Creativity and its link with intelligence
topics.h: List as many uses of a newspaper as you can in one minute. Wrapping, fanning, kite-making, papier-mâché... That's a creativity test, and there's no single right answer.
p: Creativity is the ability to produce ideas, objects or problem solutions that are novel (new) and appropriate (useful).

Creativity varies in level (from everyday creativity to the rare genius) and in domain (writing, painting, science, business). Heredity sets limits, but environment — opportunities, encouragement, freedom and training — strongly shapes how creativity develops.

Creativity tests use open-ended questions with no single correct answer (divergent thinking); intelligence tests mostly have one right answer (convergent thinking). Divergent thinking is scored on fluency (number of ideas), flexibility (variety of categories), originality (unusual ideas) and elaboration (detail added).

Relationship: a certain level of intelligence is needed for creativity, but beyond that level, high intelligence does not ensure high creativity — so a high-IQ person may not be very creative, and the correlation between the two is modest.
Indian psychologists such as Baqer Mehdi and Passi, along with Torrance and Guilford, developed creativity tests.

ex.q: In 2 minutes, Ishaan lists 12 uses of a brick, covering building, weights, doorstops, art and garden borders, including 'grind into red powder for a Holi rangoli'. Which scores are high?
st: Many ideas (12) → fluency.
Several different categories (building, weights, art, garden) → flexibility.
An unusual idea (rangoli powder) → originality.
ex.a: Fluency, flexibility and originality.

topics.rl: ISRO's Mangalyaan reached Mars orbit on a famously small budget by finding novel and appropriate engineering solutions — creativity is not only for artists.

rv.summary: Creativity is the ability to produce novel and appropriate ideas or products. It varies in level and domain, is shaped by heredity and environment, and is tested by divergent thinking (fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration).

High IQ does not guarantee high creativity
Creativity tests are divergent; intelligence tests are mostly convergent

topics.t: The concept of self and identity
topics.h: Write 'I am...' ten times and finish each line. Your answers — 'I am Ananya', 'I am a Malayali', 'I am a good singer' — reveal how you see your self.
p: Self is the totality of a person's conscious experiences, ideas, thoughts and feelings with regard to herself or himself. Personality refers to our characteristic ways of responding to people and situations.
A newborn has no clear sense of self; the self develops gradually through interaction with parents, family, friends, teachers and others.

Personal identity: attributes that make you different from others (name, abilities, beliefs, potentials). Social identity: aspects that link you to a social or cultural group (for example, 'I am from Assam', 'I am a member of the school NCC unit').
Self as subject: the self as an active agent that knows and acts ('I am planning my day'). Self as object: the self as the focus of observation ('I am a sensitive person').

Personal self: concern with oneself — personal needs, freedom, responsibility and achievement. Social self: emphasis on relations with others — cooperation, unity, sacrifice, sharing; also called the familial or relational self.

ex.q: Classify each statement: (a) 'I am a fast learner', (b) 'I am a member of the school choir', (c) 'I give up my comfort to support my family'.
st: (a) An attribute that makes the person distinct → personal identity.
(b) Links the person to a group → social identity.
(c) Values sacrifice for family → social (familial) self.
ex.a: (a) Personal identity, (b) Social identity, (c) Social/familial self.

topics.rl: In many Indian joint families, decisions about careers or weddings are discussed together. That emphasis on 'we' reflects a strong social or relational self.

rv.summary: The self is the totality of a person's conscious thoughts and feelings about herself or himself, built through social interaction. It includes personal and social identity, self as subject and object, and the personal and social self.

remember: Self: totality of conscious experiences, ideas, thoughts and feelings about oneself

'I am a calm person' is self as object, not subject

topics.t: Self-concept, self-esteem and self-efficacy
topics.h: 'I'm just not a maths person.' Those six words can shape years of effort. Psychologists study three linked ideas behind such beliefs.
p: Self-concept is the way we perceive ourselves and the ideas we hold about our competencies and attributes. It can be positive or negative and covers areas like academic, social and physical domains.

Self-esteem is the value judgement we make about ourselves. By about 6–7 years, children judge themselves in academic competence, social competence, physical/athletic competence and physical appearance; these become more refined with age.

High self-esteem in academics is linked with better school performance; low self-esteem is linked with anxiety, depression and antisocial behaviour. Warm, positive parenting supports healthy self-esteem.

Self-efficacy (Albert Bandura, social learning theory): the belief that one can control events and outcomes in one's life through one's own actions, rather than luck or fate. High self-efficacy leads people to try harder and persist.
Self-efficacy can be built through positive models, encouragement and one's own experiences of success — a link to observational learning.

ex.q: Sneha says, 'I'm good at science' (A), 'I feel proud of myself as a student' (B) and 'If I practise, I can definitely crack this tough problem' (C). Label each.
st: (A) A perception of one's competence → self-concept.
(B) A value judgement about oneself → self-esteem.
(C) Belief in one's ability to achieve an outcome through effort → self-efficacy.
ex.a: A: self-concept, B: self-esteem, C: self-efficacy.

topics.rl: When Indian athletes like Neeraj Chopra win, young javelin throwers across villages start believing 'I can do it too'. Seeing a model succeed raises self-efficacy.

rv.summary: Self-concept is how we see our competencies; self-esteem is the value judgement we make about ourselves; self-efficacy (Bandura) is the belief that our own actions can control outcomes.

Self-efficacy is not luck or fate
Low self-esteem is linked with anxiety, depression and antisocial behaviour, so self-esteem does relate to behaviour

topics.t: Self-regulation, self-control and culture and self
topics.h: Your phone buzzes during board-exam prep. Scroll now, or study and enjoy the reel later? Saying 'later' is a classic self-regulation skill.
p: Self-regulation is our ability to organise and monitor our own behaviour. People high on self-monitoring are sensitive to situational demands and adjust their behaviour.
Delay of gratification — learning to put off the satisfaction of a need — is a key part of self-control and is often called 'will power'.

Psychological techniques of self-control: (1) observation of own behaviour (tracking what you actually do), (2) self-instruction (telling yourself what to do), (3) self-reinforcement (rewarding yourself with something pleasant after desired behaviour).
Indian cultural traditions offer ways of self-regulation, such as fasting (vrata or roza) and non-attachment to worldly things (detachment).

Culture and self: in the Indian view, the boundary between self and others is flexible — the self can expand to include family and community. In the Western view, the boundary is relatively fixed. Western cultures are mostly individualistic; many Asian cultures, including India, are more collectivistic.

ex.q: Aditya writes down how many hours he really studies (1), tells himself 'Finish two chapters first' (2), and allows himself a cricket match only after finishing (3). Name the techniques.
st: (1) Recording one's own actual behaviour = observation of own behaviour.
(2) Giving oneself instructions = self-instruction.
(3) Reward after the desired behaviour = self-reinforcement.
ex.a: (1) Observation of own behaviour, (2) Self-instruction, (3) Self-reinforcement.

topics.rl: Many Indian students keep a study tracker and reward themselves with a chai break or a match after a target — a home-grown use of self-observation and self-reinforcement.

rv.summary: Self-regulation is the ability to organise and monitor one's own behaviour. Self-control uses delay of gratification and techniques like observation of own behaviour, self-instruction and self-reinforcement; Indian traditions add fasting and non-attachment.
focus: Indian vs Western view of the self
remember: Delay of gratification = will power
Techniques: observation of own behaviour, self-instruction, self-reinforcement
Indian self: flexible boundary; Western self: relatively fixed boundary
traps: Don't confuse self-instruction (telling yourself what to do) with self-reinforcement (rewarding yourself)
Recording behaviour is observation, not reinforcement
The Indian self-boundary is flexible, not rigid

topics.t: Personality: meaning and early type approaches
topics.h: Roman actors wore masks called 'persona' to show their roles. Our word 'personality' comes from that mask — but personality is far more than what shows on the surface.
p: Personality comes from the Latin word 'persona', the mask used by actors in Roman theatre. It refers to our characteristic ways of responding to individuals and situations.

Characteristics: it has both physical and psychological components; its main features are relatively stable across time and consistent across situations; yet it is dynamic, changing in response to internal or external demands.
Studying personality helps us understand and predict behaviour and helps in guidance, selection and therapy.
Type approaches group people into types. Hippocrates proposed four types based on bodily fluids (humours): sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric and melancholic.

Charak Samhita (Ayurveda) classifies people by three humoral elements, the tridosha: vata, pitta and kapha. The theory of trigunas describes sattva (cleanliness, truthfulness, discipline, detachment), rajas (intense activity, desire for sense gratification, envy, materialism) and tamas (anger, arrogance, laziness, helplessness); all three are present in everyone in different degrees.

ex.q: A person is described as disciplined, truthful and detached from material gains. Which guna is dominant?
st: Sattva includes cleanliness, truthfulness, dutifulness, detachment and discipline.
Rajas involves intense activity and desire; tamas involves anger and laziness.
So the description fits sattva.
ex.a: Sattva.

topics.rl: The Ayurveda ideas of vata, pitta and kapha still appear in Indian wellness talk today — they are one of the oldest type approaches to personality.

rv.summary: Personality, from the Latin 'persona' (mask), is our characteristic way of responding to people and situations: stable yet dynamic. Early type approaches include Hippocrates' four humours, Charak Samhita's tridosha and the trigunas.

Tridosha: vata, pitta, kapha
Sattva: truthfulness, discipline, detachment; Rajas: activity, desire, envy; Tamas: anger, arrogance, laziness
traps: Don't confuse tridosha (vata, pitta, kapha) with trigunas (sattva, rajas, tamas)
Everyone has all three gunas in different degrees
Personality is relatively stable but not fixed forever

topics.t: Body types, introverts–extraverts and Type A/B/C/D
topics.h: Always rushing, impatient in a queue, checking the time every minute? Researchers found such 'Type A' behaviour linked with heart disease.
p: William Sheldon linked body build with temperament: endomorph (fat, soft, round — relaxed and sociable), mesomorph (strong, muscular, rectangular — energetic and courageous) and ectomorph (thin, long, fragile — brainy, artistic and introverted). Body-build types are poor predictors of behaviour.
Carl Jung grouped people into introverts (prefer to be alone, shy, withdraw under stress) and extraverts (sociable, outgoing, seek people when stressed).

Friedman and Rosenman described Type-A personality: high motivation, impatience, feeling short of time, always in a hurry, burdened with work. Type-A people are more prone to hypertension and coronary heart disease (CHD). Type-B is the absence of Type-A traits.
Morris suggested Type-C (cooperative, unassertive, patient, suppress negative emotions such as anger, comply with authority; prone to cancer) and Type-D (prone to depression).
Type approaches are simple and easy to use, but people rarely fit neatly into a single type; behaviour is more complex and variable.

ex.q: Vikram eats lunch while answering emails, honks repeatedly in traffic and feels he never has enough time. Which type is he, and what health risk is linked to it?
st: Impatience, hurry and time pressure are Type-A features (Friedman and Rosenman).
Type-A is associated with hypertension and coronary heart disease.
ex.a: Type-A; higher risk of hypertension and coronary heart disease.

topics.rl: Mumbai's corporate workers racing for the 8:12 local while answering calls are textbook Type-A behaviour — doctors in metros increasingly see stress-linked heart problems in young adults.

rv.summary: Type approaches sort people into categories: Sheldon's body types, Jung's introverts and extraverts, and Type-A (linked to heart disease), Type-B, Type-C (cancer-prone) and Type-D (depression-prone). They are simple, but people rarely fit one type.
focus: Type-A, B, C and D and their health links
remember: Endomorph: round, relaxed; mesomorph: muscular, energetic; ectomorph: thin, artistic
Type-A (Friedman and Rosenman): hypertension and CHD
Type-C (Morris): cancer; Type-D: depression
traps: Type-A is linked with heart disease, not cancer
Types are categories; traits are continuous dimensions
Jung, not Eysenck, first grouped introverts and extraverts

topics.t: Trait theories: Allport, Cattell, Eysenck and the Big Five
topics.h: Describe your best friend in five words. Chances are your words map onto just five big dimensions that psychologists found across cultures, including India.
p: Traits are relatively enduring attributes on which people differ (such as honesty or sociability). Unlike types, traits are dimensions on which everyone can be placed.

Gordon Allport: cardinal traits (highly generalised; the goal around which a whole life revolves, e.g. Mahatma Gandhi's non-violence), central traits (less pervasive but common, e.g. honest, punctual) and secondary traits (least generalised, e.g. 'likes mangoes').

Raymond Cattell used factor analysis to find source traits (stable building blocks of personality) and surface traits (resulting from interactions of source traits). His 16 Personality Factor Questionnaire (16 PF) is widely used.

Hans Eysenck: two broad, biologically based dimensions — neuroticism vs emotional stability, and extraversion vs introversion; later a third, psychoticism vs sociability. Measured by the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ).
Five-Factor Model (Paul Costa and Robert McCrae): openness to experience, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism and conscientiousness (OCEAN). It has been found across cultures, including India.

ex.q: Riya is curious, plans her work carefully, is talkative, kind to everyone, and stays calm under pressure. Rate her on the Big Five.
st: Curious → high openness.
Plans carefully → high conscientiousness.
Talkative → high extraversion.
Kind → high agreeableness.
Calm under pressure → low neuroticism.
ex.a: High O, C, E and A; low N.

topics.rl: Some Indian companies use personality questionnaires like the 16 PF or Big Five-based tools when hiring, for example looking for conscientiousness in roles such as auditing.

rv.summary: Trait theories place everyone on dimensions. Allport described cardinal, central and secondary traits; Cattell found source and surface traits (16 PF); Eysenck proposed neuroticism, extraversion and psychoticism; Costa and McCrae gave the Big Five (OCEAN).

Big Five: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism
traps: A minor preference is a secondary, not cardinal, trait
High neuroticism means anxious and moody, not calm

topics.t: Freud: levels of consciousness and structure of personality
topics.h: You call your teacher 'Mummy' by mistake and the class giggles. Freud would say your unconscious just slipped out!
p: Sigmund Freud described three levels of consciousness: conscious (thoughts and feelings we are currently aware of), preconscious (material we can become aware of if we attend to it) and unconscious (thoughts and desires we are unaware of, including instinctive drives and unacceptable wishes). He used free association and dream analysis to study the unconscious.
Id: the source of instinctual energy, seeking immediate gratification of primitive needs, sexual desires and aggressive impulses; it works on the pleasure principle and ignores morality and reality.
Ego: grows out of the id and satisfies its needs in socially appropriate ways; it works on the reality principle and is often called the executive of personality.
Superego: the moral branch, the internalised values and standards (often from parents); it works on the moral principle and judges whether gratification is right or wrong.
Libido is the instinctual life force that energises the id (linked to Eros, the life instinct). Freud later also proposed Thanatos, the death instinct.

ex.q: Ravi sees an unattended expensive pen. One part of him wants to grab it, another says 'Someone may see you', and a third says 'Stealing is wrong'. Identify each.
st: Wanting it immediately = id (pleasure principle).
Thinking about real consequences = ego (reality principle).
Judging it morally wrong = superego (moral principle).
ex.a: Id: 'grab it'; Ego: 'someone may see'; Superego: 'stealing is wrong'.

topics.rl: In a group chat argument, the id wants to send an angry reply, the superego says 'Be respectful', and the ego drafts a calm message — Freud's three systems at work on WhatsApp.

rv.summary: Freud described conscious, preconscious and unconscious levels. Personality has the id (pleasure principle), ego (reality principle, the executive) and superego (moral principle), energised by libido.

remember: Id: pleasure principle
Ego: reality principle, executive of personality
Superego: moral principle, internalised values
Libido: life energy (Eros); Thanatos: death instinct

Preconscious material can be recalled with attention; unconscious material cannot easily be
Libido is not Thanatos

topics.t: Defence mechanisms and psychosexual stages
topics.h: Failed a test? 'The paper was unfair anyway!' That convenient excuse might be your ego defending itself.
p: When the ego cannot balance id, superego and reality, anxiety results. Defence mechanisms reduce anxiety by distorting reality. Everyone uses them sometimes; relying heavily on them is unhealthy.

Repression (the most common): anxiety-provoking thoughts are pushed into the unconscious. Projection: attributing one's own unacceptable traits to others. Denial: totally refusing to accept reality. Reaction formation: behaving opposite to one's true feelings. Rationalisation: giving a reasonable-sounding excuse for unreasonable feelings or behaviour.

Psychosexual stages: oral (first year; pleasure through the mouth), anal (about 2–3 years; toilet training), phallic (about 4–5 years; Oedipus complex in boys, Electra complex in girls, resolved by identifying with the same-sex parent), latency (about 7 years to puberty; urges are dormant, energy goes into social and school activities), genital (adolescence onwards; mature sexuality).

Fixation: getting stuck at an earlier stage because its conflict was not resolved. Regression: going back to an earlier stage's behaviour under stress (for example, an older child starting thumb-sucking when a new sibling arrives).

ex.q: Sumit, who strongly dislikes his new classmate, is extremely sweet and overly praising towards him. Which defence mechanism is this?
st: His true feeling is dislike.
His behaviour is the opposite — exaggerated friendliness.
Behaving opposite to true feelings = reaction formation.
ex.a: Reaction formation.

topics.rl: After a big loss, a team captain saying 'The pitch suited them, we weren't even trying hard' may be rationalising — it protects self-esteem but blocks learning.

rv.summary: Defence mechanisms reduce anxiety by distorting reality: repression, projection, denial, reaction formation and rationalisation. Freud's psychosexual stages are oral, anal, phallic, latency and genital; fixation and regression link to them.

topics.t: Post-Freudian approaches and criticisms
topics.h: Freud's students didn't just copy him — they argued with him. Their disagreements gave us ideas like the inferiority complex and the identity crisis.
p: Carl Jung — analytical psychology: personality has competing forces within the individual. Besides the personal unconscious, there is a collective unconscious shared by all humanity, containing archetypes (primordial images, such as the mother or the hero, seen in myths and dreams).

Karen Horney stressed social and cultural factors. Parental indifference, discouragement and erratic behaviour can make a child feel insecure — basic anxiety — and resentful (basic hostility). She also challenged Freud's view of women.

Alfred Adler — individual psychology: behaviour is purposeful and goal-directed. Feelings of inadequacy create an inferiority complex; striving for superiority to overcome it drives personality development.

Erich Fromm saw humans as basically social beings; qualities such as the desire for freedom, justice and truth develop through relationships with others. Erik Erikson stressed rational, conscious ego processes and psychosocial development, including the identity crisis of adolescence.

Criticisms of psychodynamic theories: based mainly on case studies without a strong scientific base; small, unusual samples; concepts that are hard to define and test; and Freud's use of males as the prototype, neglecting women.

ex.q: A 16-year-old keeps asking, 'Who am I? What do I want to become?' and tries out new interests and styles. Which theorist's idea fits best?
st: The question is about forming a sense of identity in adolescence.
Erikson described the identity crisis as a key task of adolescence.
ex.a: Erik Erikson's identity crisis.

topics.rl: Similar hero stories — a brave hero, a wise mentor, a final battle — appear in the Ramayana, Greek myths and modern films. Jung would point to archetypes from the collective unconscious.

rv.summary: Post-Freudians include Jung (collective unconscious, archetypes), Horney (basic anxiety), Adler (inferiority complex, striving for superiority), Fromm (humans as social beings) and Erikson (identity crisis). Psychodynamic theories are criticised as weakly scientific.

remember: Jung: analytical psychology, collective unconscious, archetypes
Horney: basic anxiety and basic hostility

traps: The inferiority complex is Adler's, not Jung's
The collective unconscious holds archetypes, not personal memories
Freud relied on case studies, not large random surveys

topics.t: Behavioural, cultural and humanistic approaches
topics.h: Is your personality what you learned, what your community's way of life demanded, or the person you're striving to become? Three approaches give three answers.
p: Behavioural approach: personality is the person's learned responses to the environment. Its core elements are stimulus, response and reinforcement (for example, hunger is the stimulus, eating the response, satisfaction the reinforcement). Classical conditioning (Pavlov), operant conditioning (Skinner) and observational learning (Bandura) all shape personality.
Cultural approach: personality traits are adaptations to the ecology and culture of a group. A group's economic maintenance system — how it earns its living — shapes valued traits.

In hunting-gathering, nomadic communities (for example, the Birhor of Jharkhand's forest regions), skills like independence, autonomy and achievement are valued; in settled agricultural societies, obedience, nurturance and responsibility are emphasised.

Humanistic approach — Carl Rogers: the fully functioning person; the self-concept; real self (what we are) vs ideal self (what we would like to be). A small gap brings happiness; a large gap brings dissatisfaction. Unconditional positive regard helps build a healthy self-concept.

Abraham Maslow: self-actualisation is the state of reaching one's fullest potential. Self-actualised, healthy people accept themselves and others, are realistic, creative, autonomous and capable of deep relationships and peak experiences.

ex.q: Kavya dreams of being a confident public speaker (ideal self) but sees herself as shy and hesitant (real self). According to Rogers, what will she feel, and what helps?
st: Real self (shy) is far from ideal self (confident speaker).
A large real–ideal gap leads to dissatisfaction and unhappiness.
Unconditional positive regard from others helps her accept herself and close the gap.
ex.a: She will feel dissatisfied; unconditional positive regard and acceptance help.

topics.rl: When a coach praises a young player only when she wins, love feels conditional. Rogers argued that accepting the person regardless of results builds healthier self-esteem — something good Indian sports academies now try.

rv.summary: The behavioural approach sees personality as learned (stimulus, response, reinforcement); the cultural approach as adaptation to ecology and livelihood; the humanistic approach stresses Rogers' real and ideal self with unconditional positive regard, and Maslow's self-actualisation.

Traits valued in hunting-gathering vs agricultural societies

Agricultural: obedience, nurturance, responsibility; hunting-gathering: independence, autonomy
Rogers: small real–ideal gap = happiness

Praise-based learning is operant, not classical, conditioning

topics.t: Assessing personality: self-report measures
topics.h: Question: 'I always tell the truth.' Tick yes or no. Would everyone answer honestly? That's the central problem of self-report tests.
p: Personality assessment helps understand and predict behaviour with minimum error, for purposes such as diagnosis, training, placement and counselling.

Self-report measures are fairly structured tests where people answer about themselves, often on rating scales. The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI), developed by Hathaway and McKinley to aid psychiatric diagnosis, is widely used; MMPI-2 has 567 statements and 10 subscales. In India, Mallick and Joshi developed the Jodhpur Multiphasic Personality Inventory (JMPI) along MMPI lines.

The Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ) assesses dimensions such as extraversion–introversion, emotional stability–neuroticism and psychoticism. Cattell's 16 PF measures 16 personality factors and is used with high school students, college students and adults; Indian versions exist.
Problems: social desirability — answering in a socially acceptable way rather than truthfully; acquiescence — tendency to agree ('yes') with items regardless of their content.

ex.q: A student answers 'yes' to almost every item, even to contradictory items such as 'I enjoy parties' and 'I avoid parties'. Which problem is this?
st: Agreeing with items regardless of content = acquiescence.
Contradictory 'yes' answers show the response is not based on the item's meaning.
ex.a: Acquiescence.

topics.rl: In job applications, candidates may tick 'I never lose my temper' to look good. Recruiters using personality questionnaires watch out for this social desirability bias.

rv.summary: Self-report measures are structured tests where people describe themselves, such as the MMPI (MMPI-2: 567 items), JMPI, EPQ and 16 PF. Their main problems are social desirability and acquiescence.

topics.t: Projective techniques
topics.h: Look at a cloud. One friend sees a dragon, another a dancing girl. Projective tests use exactly this: ambiguous pictures to reveal hidden feelings.
p: Projective techniques are based on psychoanalytic theory: when given an ambiguous or unstructured stimulus, a person projects unconscious feelings, desires and needs onto it. Responses are interpreted by trained experts; scoring is complex and less objective.

Rorschach Inkblot Test (Hermann Rorschach): 10 symmetrical inkblots — five black and white, two with some red, three in pastel colours. Two phases: performance proper (the person says what they see) and inquiry (a detailed report of the responses).
Thematic Apperception Test (TAT; Morgan and Murray, 1935): 30 black-and-white picture cards and one blank card; the person makes up stories. Uma Chaudhury developed an Indian adaptation.
Rosenzweig's Picture-Frustration Study (P-F Study) uses cartoon-like pictures of frustrating situations to assess how people express aggression; Pareek adapted it for India.

Sentence Completion Test: incomplete sentences (e.g., 'My father...') reveal attitudes, motives and conflicts. Draw-a-Person Test: the person draws a person, then one of the opposite sex, and makes up a story about them.

ex.q: A psychologist shows Neel a card with a blurry picture of a boy sitting near a broken violin and asks him to tell a story about what led up to it and how it ends. Which test is this?
st: Picture cards + making up a story about what happened, what is happening and what will happen.
This is the method of the Thematic Apperception Test.
ex.a: Thematic Apperception Test (TAT).

topics.rl: Clinical psychologists at institutes like NIMHANS may use projective tests alongside interviews, never alone, because scoring them requires extensive training.

rv.summary: Projective techniques use ambiguous stimuli onto which people project unconscious material. They include the Rorschach (10 inkblots), TAT (30 cards + 1 blank), Rosenzweig's P-F Study, sentence completion and Draw-a-Person; interpretation needs trained experts.

topics.t: Behavioural analysis: interviews, ratings, nominations and situational tests
topics.h: A teacher rates a student 'excellent' in every trait just because she is great at cricket. That single bright spot is colouring everything — psychologists call it the halo effect.
p: Behavioural analysis uses a person's behaviour in real situations to assess personality.

Interview: structured (specific questions in a set order) or unstructured (flexible questions guided by the person's responses). Observation by trained observers gives rich data but is time-consuming and can be influenced by the observer.

Behavioural ratings: raters (teachers, peers, supervisors) place people into categories or rate them on traits. Errors: halo effect (a single favourable or unfavourable trait colours all ratings), middle category bias (rating everyone in the middle, avoiding extremes) and extreme response bias (rating at the extreme ends).
Nominations: peers who know a person well nominate people with certain qualities; useful and fairly reliable, though personal biases can creep in.
Situational tests: the person is observed in a created situation; the most common is the situational stress test, where tasks are done with others who have been instructed to be non-cooperative.

ex.q: An interviewer rates a well-dressed candidate highly on honesty, intelligence and teamwork without evidence. Which error occurred?
st: One favourable feature (appearance) influenced ratings on unrelated traits.
That is the halo effect.
ex.a: Halo effect.

topics.rl: Services Selection Boards (SSB) that pick officers for the Indian Armed Forces use group tasks and situational tests, observing how candidates act under pressure, along with interviews.

rv.summary: Behavioural analysis assesses personality from behaviour in real situations through interviews, observation, behavioural ratings, nominations and situational tests. Ratings suffer from the halo effect, middle category bias and extreme response bias.

topics.t: What is stress? Eustress, distress and cognitive appraisal
topics.h: Two students get the same board timetable. One says 'Finally, a chance to show what I've got!' The other says 'I'm doomed.' Same event — very different stress. Why?
p: Life brings challenges; how we adjust to them affects our well-being. Stress is the pattern of responses an organism makes to a stimulus event that disturbs its equilibrium and exceeds its ability to cope. The event causing it is a stressor.
The word stress comes from the Latin 'strictus', meaning tight or narrow (and the verb 'stringere', to tighten).
Hans Selye used 'eustress' for a healthy, positive level of stress that motivates and improves performance; 'distress' is excessive, harmful stress.

Richard Lazarus's cognitive theory: primary appraisal judges a new or changing event as positive, neutral or negative; negative events are judged for harm (damage already done), threat (possible future damage) or challenge (confidence of overcoming it, with possible positive outcomes).

Secondary appraisal is the assessment of one's coping abilities and resources — whether they will be enough to deal with the harm, threat or challenge. Stress is felt when demands seem to exceed resources.

ex.q: Ayesha learns that her science practical exam is next week. She thinks 'This could go badly' (1), then 'But I've practised every experiment and my teacher will help' (2). Label the two appraisals and predict her stress.
st: (1) Judging the event as possibly harmful in the future = primary appraisal of threat.
(2) Evaluating her preparation and teacher's support = secondary appraisal of coping resources.
Resources seem adequate, so stress is likely to be manageable — even eustress.
ex.a: (1) Primary appraisal (threat); (2) Secondary appraisal; moderate, manageable stress.

topics.rl: Before a World Cup final, a fast bowler may feel the pressure as a challenge rather than a threat. Sports psychologists working with Indian teams train players to re-appraise pressure exactly this way.

rv.summary: Stress is the pattern of responses to a stressor that disturbs equilibrium and exceeds coping ability. Eustress is healthy stress; distress is harmful. Lazarus's primary appraisal judges harm, threat or challenge; secondary appraisal judges coping resources.

topics.t: Signs, symptoms and types of stress
topics.h: Headache, snapping at your sibling, and staring at the same page for 20 minutes — three different signs, one possible cause: stress.
p: Signs and symptoms of stress can be physical (headaches, fatigue, sleep problems), emotional (irritability, anxiety, mood swings) and behavioural (changes in eating, withdrawal, poor work). Each person shows stress in their own way.

Physical and environmental stress: physical demands change the body's state (overexertion, poor nutrition, injury, lack of sleep); environmental stressors are unavoidable aspects of surroundings (air pollution, crowding, noise, summer heat, winter cold) and disasters (floods, earthquakes, fire).

Psychological stress comes from within: frustration (blocking of needs and motives), conflicts (between two or more incompatible needs or motives), internal pressures (beliefs like 'I must do everything perfectly') and social pressures (people making excessive demands on us).

Social stress is induced by interaction with other people — death or illness in the family, strained relationships, trouble with neighbours. Even a party can be stressful for someone who prefers solitude.

ex.q: Classify: (a) Delhi's winter smog, (b) wanting to join both the dance club and the coding club that meet at the same time, (c) a quarrel with a close friend.
st: (a) Unavoidable surroundings = environmental stress.
(b) Two incompatible motives = conflict, a psychological stress.
(c) Arises from interaction with others = social stress.
ex.a: (a) Environmental, (b) Psychological (conflict), (c) Social.

topics.rl: Mumbai's packed local trains, Chennai's summer heat and Assam's annual floods are everyday reminders of environmental stress for millions of Indians.

rv.summary: Stress shows physical, emotional and behavioural signs. Its types are physical and environmental stress, psychological stress (frustration, conflict, internal and social pressures) and social stress from interactions with others.
