topics.t: Sources of stress: life events, hassles and traumatic events
topics.h: Getting married, changing city, a new job — happy events! Yet each one can raise your stress score on a famous scale.
p: Life events: major or minor, sudden or gradual changes such as moving house, a new job, marriage or loss of a loved one. Holmes and Rahe's Social Readjustment Rating Scale (SRRS) gives each event a value based on how much readjustment it needs; death of a spouse ranks highest.
Both pleasant and unpleasant events require readjustment and add to stress; a high total score within a short period is linked with a higher risk of illness.

Hassles: everyday irritations of daily life — noisy surroundings, commuting, water or power cuts, traffic jams, quarrelsome neighbours. The more hassles people report, the lower their psychological well-being tends to be.
Traumatic events: extreme events such as fire, train or road accidents, robbery, earthquakes or tsunamis. Their effects can last a long time as anxiety, flashbacks, nightmares and intrusive thoughts.

ex.q: In one month, Prakash shifts to Hyderabad for a new job, gets married, and deals with daily traffic jams. Which sources of stress are present?
st: Shifting city, new job and marriage = life events (all need readjustment, even happy ones).
Daily traffic jams = hassles.
ex.a: Life events (relocation, new job, marriage) and hassles (traffic).

topics.rl: Bengaluru's notorious traffic, daily power cuts in some towns and long ration queues are classic hassles; the 2004 tsunami and the Kedarnath floods of 2013 were traumatic events whose effects lasted years.

rv.summary: Sources of stress are life events (changes needing readjustment, measured by Holmes and Rahe's SRRS), daily hassles and traumatic events. Both pleasant and unpleasant changes add to stress.
focus: The SRRS and why even happy events are stressful
Hassles vs life events vs traumatic events
remember: SRRS: Holmes and Rahe; death of a spouse ranks highest
Hassles: everyday irritations; more hassles → lower well-being
Trauma effects: anxiety, flashbacks, nightmares, intrusive thoughts
traps: Pleasant events like marriage also count as stressful life events
Hassles are frequent and small, not rare and major
Several life events in a short time raise illness risk

topics.t: Effects of stress on mind, body and behaviour
topics.h: During exam week you forget a formula you knew perfectly, sleep badly and crave junk food. Stress touches emotions, body, thinking and behaviour all at once.
p: Emotional effects: mood swings, erratic behaviour, anxiety, depression, feelings of alienation, and physical and mental tension.

Physiological effects: the adrenal glands release stress hormones such as epinephrine (adrenaline) and norepinephrine (noradrenaline), and also cortisol. Effects include faster heart rate, expansion of air passages, constriction of blood vessels and slowing of digestion.

Cognitive effects: poor concentration and reduced short-term memory capacity. Behavioural effects: disrupted sleep, disturbed eating, more caffeine or other stimulants, increased absenteeism and reduced work performance.
Burnout is a state of physical, emotional and psychological exhaustion that follows prolonged, high stress.
Chronic stress is linked with illnesses such as coronary heart disease, high blood pressure, ulcers and asthma, as well as lowered immunity.

ex.q: A software engineer has worked 80-hour weeks for a year. He now feels drained, cynical about work and physically tired all the time. What is this state called?
st: Prolonged, intense stress at work.
Physical, emotional and psychological exhaustion together.
This is burnout.
ex.a: Burnout.

topics.rl: Doctors and nurses during the COVID-19 waves in India reported high levels of burnout — long shifts and constant pressure exhausted body and mind. If stress ever feels overwhelming, Tele-MANAS (14416) offers free, confidential support.

rv.summary: Stress has emotional (mood swings, anxiety), physiological (epinephrine, norepinephrine, cortisol; faster heart, slowed digestion), cognitive (poor concentration and memory) and behavioural (sleep, eating, absenteeism) effects. Prolonged stress causes burnout and illness.
focus: Classifying an effect as emotional, physiological, cognitive or behavioural
Stress hormones and their bodily effects
remember: Hormones: epinephrine (adrenaline), norepinephrine (noradrenaline), cortisol
Burnout: physical, emotional and psychological exhaustion
Chronic stress: heart disease, high blood pressure, ulcers, asthma
traps: Poor concentration is cognitive, not behavioural
Stress slows digestion and raises heart rate, not the reverse
Burnout is exhaustion, not a short burst of excitement

topics.t: General Adaptation Syndrome (Selye)
topics.h: First the panic, then the long grind, then the crash. Hans Selye mapped this three-stage pattern in the body's response to prolonged stress.
p: Hans Selye studied animals exposed to stressors such as high temperature, X-rays and insulin injections, and patients with injuries and illnesses. He found a similar pattern of bodily response, the General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS).

Stage 1 — Alarm reaction: the presence of a stressor activates the adrenal–pituitary–cortex system and the sympathetic nervous system; hormones are released and the body's defences are mobilised for 'fight or flight'.
Stage 2 — Resistance: if stress continues, the body tries to cope; the parasympathetic nervous system calls for more careful use of the body's resources.
Stage 3 — Exhaustion: continued exposure to the same or additional stressors drains the body's resources, and stress-related illnesses (such as high blood pressure) become more likely.
Criticism: GAS gives a very limited role to psychological factors such as cognitive appraisal, and people respond differently to the same stressor.

ex.q: A farmer faces a long drought. In week 1 he panics (racing heart). For months he works extra hours digging wells. After a year he falls ill. Map these to GAS.
st: Week 1: sudden mobilisation of the body = alarm reaction.
Months of effort to cope = resistance.
Resources depleted, illness = exhaustion.
ex.a: Alarm → Resistance → Exhaustion.

topics.rl: Indian Army soldiers posted at Siachen face extreme cold for long periods. Postings there are kept short and rotated; in GAS terms, this limits how long the body must stay in the resistance stage before exhaustion can set in.

rv.summary: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome has three stages: alarm reaction (defences mobilised), resistance (coping with continuing stress) and exhaustion (resources drained, illness likely). It is criticised for neglecting appraisal.
focus: Order and features of the three GAS stages
Mapping a case to a stage
remember: GAS: alarm reaction → resistance → exhaustion (Hans Selye)
Alarm: fight or flight; resistance: parasympathetic system conserves resources; exhaustion: illness likely
traps: Don't change the order of the stages
Illness is most likely in exhaustion, not alarm
GAS gives little role to cognitive appraisal; that is its weakness

topics.t: Stress, the immune system and lifestyle
topics.h: Ever noticed how many students catch a cold right after board exams? Your mind and your immune system talk to each other.
p: Psychoneuroimmunology studies the links between the mind, the brain (nervous system) and the immune system. Stress can weaken immune functioning.
The immune system guards the body against foreign bodies (antigens) such as viruses. White blood cells (leucocytes) identify and destroy them.

Three kinds of white blood cells: T cells destroy invaders (T-helper cells increase immunological activity and are the cells attacked by HIV); B cells produce antibodies; natural killer cells fight viruses and tumours. Stress can reduce natural killer cell activity.
Stress can push people toward unhealthy lifestyles: poor nutrition, too little sleep and exercise, smoking and alcohol use — which further harm health.
Health-promoting behaviours include a balanced diet, regular exercise, enough sleep, positive thinking and supportive relationships.

ex.q: During exam season, Simran sleeps little, survives on chips and gets fever twice. Explain using psychoneuroimmunology and lifestyle.
st: Exam stress can lower immune activity (for example, natural killer cell activity).
Stress also pushed her into an unhealthy lifestyle: little sleep, poor food.
Both together raise her chances of infection.
ex.a: Stress weakened her immunity directly and indirectly through an unhealthy lifestyle.

topics.rl: Fit India and Khelo India campaigns encourage daily exercise and balanced diets — health-promoting behaviours that also act as buffers against stress.

rv.summary: Psychoneuroimmunology studies how the mind, brain and immune system interact. Stress can weaken immunity, e.g. by lowering natural killer cell activity, and can push people into unhealthy lifestyles that further harm health.
focus: The three kinds of white blood cells
Direct and indirect ways stress harms health
remember: T cells destroy invaders; T-helper cells are attacked by HIV
B cells produce antibodies
Natural killer cells fight viruses and tumours; stress lowers their activity
traps: B cells, not T cells, produce antibodies
Don't use GAS stages to explain weakened immunity
Stress harms health both directly (immunity) and indirectly (lifestyle)

topics.t: Coping with stress: strategies and styles
topics.h: Bad marks in a unit test. Do you (a) make a study plan, (b) cry it out with a friend, or (c) binge-watch a web series and pretend it didn't happen? Each is a coping strategy.
p: Coping is a dynamic, situation-specific reaction to stress — a set of concrete responses aimed at resolving the problem and reducing stress.
Endler and Parker described three strategies. Task-oriented: getting information about the stressful situation and alternatives, setting priorities and acting directly.

Emotion-oriented: efforts to maintain hope and control emotions; venting feelings of anger and frustration; or deciding nothing can be done. Avoidance-oriented: denying or minimising the seriousness of the situation, suppressing stressful thoughts, and replacing them with self-protective thoughts (such as watching TV or calling a friend).

Lazarus and Folkman: problem-focused coping attacks the problem itself (gathering information, changing the situation, altering beliefs), while emotion-focused coping tries to limit emotional disruption with little effort to change the event.
Problem-focused strategies generally work better when the situation can be changed; emotion-focused coping is useful when it cannot (for example, after a loss).

ex.q: Classify: (a) Mohit asks his teacher which topics he got wrong and makes a revision plan; (b) Sara tells herself 'it doesn't matter, the test wasn't important' and goes out with friends.
st: (a) Gathering information and acting on the problem = task-oriented / problem-focused.
(b) Minimising the seriousness and distracting herself = avoidance-oriented.
ex.a: (a) Task-oriented (problem-focused); (b) Avoidance-oriented.

topics.rl: When a cyclone warning is issued in Odisha, families who stock supplies and move to shelters are using task-oriented coping — and Odisha's preparedness has saved thousands of lives.

rv.summary: Coping is a dynamic, situation-specific response to stress. Endler and Parker describe task-, emotion- and avoidance-oriented strategies; Lazarus and Folkman describe problem-focused and emotion-focused coping.
focus: Choosing a coping style to fit the situation
remember: Task-oriented: get information, prioritise, act directly
Emotion-oriented: manage or vent feelings
Avoidance-oriented: deny or minimise, distract oneself
Problem-focused works when the situation can change; emotion-focused when it cannot
traps: Avoidance coping is not acting directly on the problem
Don't mix up the authors: Endler and Parker vs Lazarus and Folkman
Problem-focused coping cannot undo an event like a death

topics.t: Stress management techniques
topics.h: Fighter pilots, surgeons and archers all train their nervous systems. You can too — from slow breathing to watching your own heart rate on a screen.
p: Relaxation techniques reduce symptoms of stress and lower illnesses such as high blood pressure and heart disease. Relaxation often starts with the lower body and moves up to the facial muscles, combined with slow, deep breathing.
Meditation is a yogic method of focusing attention to alter the state of consciousness — concentrating on a mantra, an object or the breath; mindful meditation trains calm awareness.

Biofeedback monitors and reduces the physiological aspects of stress by giving feedback about current physiological activity, often with relaxation training. Three stages: (1) becoming aware of a particular physiological response (e.g. heart rate), (2) learning to control it in quiet conditions, (3) transferring that control to everyday life.
Creative visualisation uses imagery and imagination (e.g. picturing a calm beach); it works best in a quiet, relaxed state with eyes closed and realistic images.

Stress inoculation training (Donald Meichenbaum), a cognitive-behavioural technique, replaces negative, irrational thoughts with positive, rational ones in three phases: assessment, stress reduction techniques, and application and follow-through. Regular exercise (walking, swimming, cycling, skipping) also acts as a stress buffer.

ex.q: Put the biofeedback stages in order for a student who gets a racing heart before presentations.
st: First, she learns to notice her heart rate rising using a monitor.
Next, she practises lowering it in a quiet room using relaxation.
Finally, she uses the same control just before real presentations.
ex.a: Awareness → control in quiet conditions → transfer to everyday life.

topics.rl: Indian archers and shooters train with breathing and visualisation routines; many schools also start the day with a short meditation or pranayama session.

rv.summary: Stress management techniques include relaxation, meditation, biofeedback (awareness, control, transfer), creative visualisation, Meichenbaum's stress inoculation training (assessment, stress reduction, application) and regular exercise.
focus: Matching each technique to its description
remember: Biofeedback: awareness → control in quiet conditions → transfer to daily life
SIT (Meichenbaum): assessment → stress reduction techniques → application and follow-through
Relaxation: lower body up to face, with deep breathing
traps: Don't confuse biofeedback (body signal feedback) with creative visualisation (imagery)
SIT replaces irrational thoughts; exercise does not
Awareness, not transfer, is the first biofeedback stage

topics.t: Hardiness and life skills: assertiveness, time management, rational thinking
topics.h: Some people seem to bounce through tough times. Suzanne Kobasa found they share three Cs — and the good news is these attitudes can be learned.
p: Stress-resistant personality — hardiness (Suzanne Kobasa): a set of beliefs about oneself, the world and how they interact. Its 3 Cs are commitment (to work, family, hobbies and social life), control (a sense of purpose and direction in life) and challenge (seeing changes as normal and positive rather than as threats).
Life skills are abilities for adaptive and positive behaviour that help us deal effectively with the demands and challenges of daily life.
Assertiveness helps us communicate our feelings, needs, wants and thoughts clearly and confidently — including the ability to say 'no', express opinions without fear and express emotions.
Time management: spend time on the things you value or that help you reach your goals; plan, prioritise and delegate, and balance work and leisure.
Rational thinking: challenge distorted thinking and irrational beliefs, drive out intrusive anxiety-provoking thoughts, and make positive statements.

ex.q: A friend keeps asking Diya to do his assignments. Write an assertive reply and name the skill.
st: Express your feeling and need clearly and respectfully.
Example: 'I understand you're busy, but I can't do your assignment. I can explain the topic if you like.'
Saying 'no' confidently without aggression = assertiveness.
ex.a: An honest, respectful 'no' — assertiveness.

topics.rl: Many Indian boards and NGOs run life-skills education in schools, often based on the WHO list of life skills, so students learn to say no to risky peer pressure and manage exam time.

rv.summary: Hardiness (Kobasa) is a stress-resistant personality with commitment, control and challenge. Life skills such as assertiveness, time management and rational thinking help us meet daily demands.
focus: Assertiveness, time management and rational thinking
Matching a problem to the life skill that helps
remember: Hardiness (Suzanne Kobasa): commitment, control, challenge
Control: sense of purpose and direction; challenge: seeing change as positive
Assertiveness: clear, confident expression, including saying no
traps: Hardiness is Kobasa's idea, not Selye's
Assertiveness is not aggression or always agreeing
'Control' in hardiness means purpose and direction, not controlling others

topics.t: Life skills: relationships, self-care and overcoming unhelpful habits
topics.h: 'I'll start studying tomorrow.' Said every day for two weeks? Procrastination is one of three unhelpful habits that quietly pile up stress.
p: Improving relationships: communication is key — listening, expressing and explaining. Avoid jealousy and sulking; respect others' feelings.

Self-care: keeping ourselves healthy and relaxed so we are prepared physically and psychologically. Slow, deep abdominal breathing helps; we can also reduce environmental stressors such as noise, pollution, poor light and clutter.
Perfectionism: wanting everything done perfectly, which leads to tiredness and stress; perfectionists find it hard to relax and are critical of themselves and others.

Avoidance: putting issues 'under the carpet' and refusing to accept or face them. Procrastination: putting off what we know we must do ('I'll do it later'), often to avoid fear of failure or rejection.

For exam stress: plan with a timetable (time management), challenge catastrophic thoughts (rational thinking), keep sleep, food and exercise regular (self-care), talk to family or friends (relationships) and break tasks into small steps to beat procrastination.

ex.q: Suggest a life-skills plan for Tanya, who is anxious about boards, studies late into the night, avoids difficult chapters and fights with her brother.
st: Time management: a realistic timetable that tackles hard chapters in small chunks (beats avoidance and procrastination).
Self-care: fixed sleep time, healthy meals, short exercise breaks.
Rational thinking: replace 'I'll fail' with 'I've prepared — I can improve step by step'.
Relationships: calm talk with her brother; seek support from parents or a teacher.
ex.a: Combine time management, self-care, rational thinking and better relationships.

topics.rl: Every board season, CBSE runs psychosocial counselling for students, and counsellors give the same advice: plan your time, sleep well, eat properly and talk to family instead of panicking.

rv.summary: Life skills also include improving relationships through communication and self-care, and overcoming unhelpful habits: perfectionism, avoidance and procrastination. Together they help manage stress such as exam stress.
focus: Communication and self-care as life skills
Building a plan for exam stress
remember: Perfectionism: wanting everything perfect → tiredness and stress
Avoidance: putting issues under the carpet
Procrastination: putting off what must be done
Self-care: deep abdominal breathing, fewer environmental stressors
traps: Don't confuse perfectionism with procrastination
Avoidance is not self-care
Waiting to feel fully motivated feeds procrastination

topics.t: Positive health, stress buffers and social support
topics.h: Health isn't just 'not being sick'. A body that works well, people who have your back, a sense of purpose — that's positive health.
p: Positive health includes a healthy body, good relationships, a sense of purpose in life, self-acceptance and resistance to illness.
Stress buffers protect us from the harmful effects of stress: a balanced diet, regular exercise, a positive attitude, positive thinking and social support.
Optimism — the tendency to expect the best possible outcomes — is linked with better psychological and physical well-being. Resilience is the ability to bounce back from adversity.

Social support is the existence and availability of people on whom we can rely, who show that they care for, value and love us. Perceived support (feeling supported) is strongly linked with well-being.

Types of social support: tangible (material help such as money, goods or services), informational (information about the stressful event, advice or tips) and emotional (reassurance that one is loved, valued and cared for).

ex.q: Classify each kind of help to Arnav, who has broken his leg before exams: (a) his friend lends him notes, (b) a senior explains which chapters carry the most marks, (c) his grandmother reassures him that he is loved no matter the result.
st: (a) Material help — notes = tangible support.
(b) Advice and information = informational support.
(c) Reassurance of love = emotional support.
ex.a: (a) Tangible, (b) Informational, (c) Emotional.

topics.rl: When Kerala faced the 2018 floods, neighbours, fishermen and volunteers provided boats, food, information and comfort — all three types of social support at once. If you ever feel overwhelmed, talking to someone you trust or calling Tele-MANAS (14416) is a strong step.

rv.summary: Positive health includes a healthy body, good relationships, purpose, self-acceptance and resistance to illness. Stress buffers like diet, exercise, positive thinking, optimism, resilience and social support (tangible, informational, emotional) protect us.
focus: The three types of social support
remember: Tangible support: material help
Informational support: advice and information
Emotional support: reassurance of love and care
Optimism: expecting the best outcomes; resilience: bouncing back
traps: Lending notes is tangible, not informational, support
Positive health is more than the absence of illness
Optimism is not ignoring problems

topics.t: What is abnormal? The four Ds and stigma
topics.h: Is a person who talks to herself on a phone headset 'abnormal'? Ten years ago people might have stared. Deciding what's a disorder is trickier than it looks.
p: Psychological disorders are patterns of behaviour, thought and emotion that cause significant distress and interfere with everyday functioning. 'Abnormal' literally means 'away from the normal'.

The four Ds: deviance (different, extreme, unusual or bizarre), distress (unpleasant and upsetting to the person and others), dysfunction (interfering with the ability to carry out daily activities in constructive ways) and danger (possibly dangerous to the person or others). Most people with psychological disorders are not dangerous.

Two approaches to abnormality: deviation from social norms (stated or unstated rules of a society) and maladaptive behaviour (behaviour that interferes with optimal functioning and growth). Many psychologists prefer the maladaptive view, since norms differ across cultures and times.

Stigma — negative labels and attitudes attached to mental illness — stops people from seeking help. Psychological disorders are not a personal failing; they are treatable, and seeking help is a sign of strength.
Using person-first, respectful language ('a person with depression', not 'a depressive') helps reduce stigma.

ex.q: A student checks the gas knob 30 times every night, cannot sleep, feels deeply upset by it and is now missing school. Which of the four Ds apply?
st: Repeating the check 30 times is unusual → deviance.
Feeling deeply upset → distress.
Missing school and sleep → dysfunction.
No risk of harm is described, so danger is not shown.
ex.a: Deviance, distress and dysfunction.

topics.rl: India's Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 protects the rights and dignity of persons with mental illness, and awareness drives in schools and colleges work to reduce stigma so people seek help early.

rv.summary: Psychological disorders are patterns of behaviour, thought and emotion causing distress and dysfunction. The four Ds are deviance, distress, dysfunction and danger. Abnormality is judged by social norms or maladaptiveness, and stigma stops people seeking help.
focus: The four Ds and spotting them in a case
Deviation from norms vs maladaptive behaviour
remember: Four Ds: deviance, distress, dysfunction, danger
Maladaptive behaviour: interferes with optimal functioning and growth
Most people with psychological disorders are not dangerous
traps: Don't assume people with disorders are dangerous
Social norms differ across cultures and times, so they are a limited test

topics.t: Historical views of abnormal behaviour
topics.h: For centuries, people with mental illness were thought to be possessed. Today we talk about genes, thoughts and society. How did that shift happen?
p: Supernatural and magical approach: abnormal behaviour was blamed on evil spirits or magic; treatment included exorcism. A shaman (a person believed to have contact with supernatural forces) acted as the medium.
Biological or organic approach: ancient Greek thinkers such as Hippocrates, Socrates and Plato held that disorders have bodily causes, much like physical illnesses.
Psychological approach: problems arise from inadequacies in the way a person thinks, feels or perceives the world.

Middle Ages: demonology and superstition dominated. Renaissance: renewed humanism and curiosity about behaviour. Age of Reason and Enlightenment (17th–18th centuries): scientific thinking and more humane treatment.

Reform movement: asylums were reformed for humane care; later, deinstitutionalisation moved patients from large hospitals to community care. The modern interactional or biopsychosocial approach holds that biological, psychological and social factors all interact.

ex.q: Arrange these views from earliest to most modern: biopsychosocial approach, demonology of the Middle Ages, Age of Reason and Enlightenment.
st: Middle Ages came first — demonology.
The Age of Reason and Enlightenment (17th–18th centuries) came later.
The biopsychosocial approach is modern.
ex.a: Demonology → Age of Reason → biopsychosocial.

topics.rl: India's Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 promotes community-based care and rights for patients — part of the worldwide move from locked asylums to humane, community treatment.

rv.summary: Views of abnormality moved from supernatural (spirits, shamans) and organic causes, through Middle Ages demonology, the Renaissance and the Age of Reason, to reform, deinstitutionalisation and today's biopsychosocial approach.
remember: Shaman: believed to contact supernatural forces
Organic approach: Hippocrates, Socrates, Plato
Deinstitutionalisation: hospital to community care
Biopsychosocial: biological + psychological + social factors interact
traps: Demonology belongs to the Middle Ages, not the Age of Reason
Deinstitutionalisation means community care, not locking patients up
The psychological approach does not blame spirits

topics.t: Classifying disorders and biological factors
topics.h: Two doctors in Delhi and Chennai see patients with similar symptoms. How do they make sure they mean the same thing when they write 'depressive disorder'? They use shared classification systems.
p: The American Psychiatric Association publishes the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders; its current edition is DSM-5.
The World Health Organization publishes the International Classification of Diseases. NCERT discusses ICD-10 (its chapter on mental and behavioural disorders); WHO has since brought ICD-11 into use.
Classification gives professionals a common language, helps in diagnosis and treatment planning, and supports research.

Biological factors: faulty genes, endocrine imbalances, malnutrition and injuries; and abnormal neurotransmitter activity. Low GABA activity is linked with anxiety, excess dopamine activity with schizophrenia, and low serotonin activity with depression. Brain structure abnormalities may also play a role.

ex.q: A researcher finds that a person's brain shows unusually low activity of the neurotransmitter GABA. Which disorder group is this most associated with?
st: GABA normally calms nerve activity.
Low GABA activity is linked with anxiety disorders.
ex.a: Anxiety disorders.

topics.rl: AIIMS and NIMHANS psychiatrists diagnose using standard criteria like ICD and DSM so that research from Bengaluru can be compared with studies from London or Tokyo.

rv.summary: Disorders are classified by DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association) and ICD (WHO), giving a common language. Biological factors include genes, endocrine imbalance, brain structure and neurotransmitters: low GABA (anxiety), excess dopamine (schizophrenia), low serotonin (depression).
remember: DSM-5: American Psychiatric Association; ICD: World Health Organization
Low GABA → anxiety; excess dopamine → schizophrenia; low serotonin → depression
traps: DSM-5 is not published by WHO
Excess dopamine, not low serotonin, is linked with schizophrenia
Irrational beliefs are a psychological, not biological, factor

topics.t: Psychological and socio-cultural factors; diathesis–stress model
topics.h: Two cousins carry the same family risk for depression. One faces years of hardship and develops it; the other doesn't. The diathesis–stress model explains why.
p: Psychodynamic model (the oldest and best known): behaviour comes from unconscious conflicts among id, ego and superego.

Behavioural model: abnormal behaviour results from learning maladaptive ways of behaving (through classical, operant or observational learning). Cognitive model: abnormal behaviour results from irrational assumptions and attitudes and unclear thinking.
Humanistic–existential model: focuses on broader aspects of human existence — humanists stress self-actualisation; existentialists stress freedom, responsibility and finding meaning.
Socio-cultural factors: war and violence, group stress, poverty and unemployment, prejudice and discrimination, family structure and communication, social networks, and societal labels and roles.

Diathesis–stress model: (1) a diathesis — a biological predisposition, which may be inherited; (2) this diathesis makes the person vulnerable to a disorder; (3) a pathogenic (harmful) stressor triggers the disorder. Both vulnerability and stressor are needed.

ex.q: Meena has a family history of anxiety (inherited vulnerability). She develops severe anxiety only after losing her job and facing debts. Explain using the diathesis–stress model.
st: Diathesis: inherited biological vulnerability for anxiety.
Pathogenic stressor: job loss and debts.
Vulnerability + stressor together produced the disorder.
ex.a: Her inherited diathesis interacted with severe stressors to trigger the disorder.

topics.rl: After disasters like the 2001 Gujarat earthquake, not everyone developed lasting distress — studies point to the mix of personal vulnerability, the severity of the stress and the support available.

rv.summary: Psychological models explain disorders through unconscious conflicts (psychodynamic), learning (behavioural), faulty thinking (cognitive) and meaning and growth (humanistic–existential). Socio-cultural factors also matter, and the diathesis–stress model combines vulnerability with a stressor.
focus: The three parts of the diathesis–stress model
remember: Psychodynamic: oldest model
Behavioural: learned maladaptive behaviour
Cognitive: irrational assumptions
Diathesis–stress: inherited vulnerability + pathogenic stressor
traps: Diathesis is the vulnerability, not the stressful event
Vulnerability alone is not enough to cause a disorder
Fear learned by watching a parent is behavioural, not psychodynamic

topics.t: Anxiety disorders
topics.h: Everyone feels butterflies before a board exam. But when worry is constant, intense and not linked to anything specific, it may be an anxiety disorder.
p: Anxiety is a diffuse, vague, very unpleasant feeling of fear and apprehension. Symptoms can include rapid heart rate, shortness of breath, sweating, dizziness, loss of appetite, sleeplessness, frequent urination and tremors.

Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD): prolonged, vague, unexplained and intense fears not attached to any particular object; worry about the future, hypervigilance and motor tension (restlessness, inability to relax).

Panic disorder: recurrent panic attacks — abrupt surges of intense anxiety with shortness of breath, dizziness, trembling, palpitations, choking, nausea, chest pain, and fear of losing control or dying.

Phobias are irrational fears of specific objects, people or situations: specific phobias (most common, e.g. of animals or enclosed spaces), social anxiety disorder (intense fear and embarrassment when dealing with others) and agoraphobia (fear of entering unfamiliar situations; some avoid leaving home).
Separation anxiety disorder: children feel excessive anxiety or even panic when separated from parents or caregivers; they may be fussy, have tantrums or refuse to go to school.

ex.q: A person feels sudden waves of terror with a pounding heart, chest pain and fear of dying, several times a month, without warning. Which disorder fits best?
st: Sudden, recurrent attacks with intense physical symptoms = panic attacks.
Recurrent panic attacks define panic disorder.
GAD is continuous vague worry, not sudden attacks.
ex.a: Panic disorder.

topics.rl: Many Indian students fear speaking in class or at interviews. When that fear becomes intense and disabling, it may be social anxiety disorder — very treatable with therapy. Tele-MANAS (14416) can guide people to help.

rv.summary: Anxiety is diffuse fear and apprehension. Anxiety disorders include generalised anxiety disorder (free-floating worry), panic disorder (recurrent panic attacks), phobias (specific, social anxiety, agoraphobia) and separation anxiety disorder.
remember: GAD: prolonged, vague fears not tied to an object; hypervigilance, motor tension
Panic disorder: recurrent sudden panic attacks
Specific phobia is the most common
Agoraphobia: fear of unfamiliar situations
traps: GAD is continuous worry, not sudden attacks
Ordinary short-lived exam nervousness is not a disorder
Agoraphobia is not the same as social anxiety disorder

topics.t: Obsessive-compulsive, related and trauma disorders
topics.h: People joke 'I'm so OCD' about tidy desks. Real OCD isn't a quirk — it's distressing thoughts and rituals that can take hours each day.
p: Obsessive behaviour is the inability to stop thinking about a particular idea or topic; these thoughts are unwanted, unpleasant and often shameful to the person.

Compulsive behaviour is the need to perform certain behaviours repeatedly, such as counting, ordering, checking, touching and washing. In obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), obsessions and compulsions take a lot of time and interfere with life.
Related disorders include hoarding disorder (difficulty discarding possessions), trichotillomania (repeated hair-pulling) and excoriation (repeated skin-picking).
Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) can follow traumatic events such as natural disasters, serious accidents or violence.
PTSD symptoms include recurrent dreams or nightmares, flashbacks, impaired concentration and emotional numbing. Treatment and support help people recover.

ex.q: Arjun keeps thinking his hands are contaminated (1) and washes them 40 times a day (2), spending hours and missing classes. Label (1) and (2).
st: (1) An unwanted, recurring thought = obsession.
(2) A repeated action to reduce the anxiety = compulsion.
Together, causing distress and dysfunction, they suggest OCD.
ex.a: (1) Obsession, (2) Compulsion.

topics.rl: After the 2013 Uttarakhand floods, mental health teams worked with survivors who had nightmares and flashbacks — classic PTSD symptoms — showing why disaster relief needs psychological care too.

rv.summary: OCD involves unwanted recurring thoughts (obsessions) and repeated actions (compulsions) that take time and disrupt life. Related disorders are hoarding, trichotillomania and excoriation. PTSD follows trauma, with nightmares, flashbacks, poor concentration and numbing.
remember: Obsession: unwanted recurring thought
Compulsion: repeated action such as checking or washing
Trichotillomania: hair-pulling; excoriation: skin-picking
PTSD: nightmares, flashbacks, poor concentration, emotional numbing
traps: Don't swap obsession (thought) and compulsion (action)
Being neat is not OCD
Trichotillomania is hair-pulling, not skin-picking

topics.t: Somatic symptom and dissociative disorders
topics.h: A person suddenly cannot move an arm, yet every medical test is normal. Another forgets who they are and turns up in a different city. The mind can affect the body and memory in surprising ways.
p: Somatic symptom and related disorders involve psychological difficulties expressed as physical symptoms without an adequate biological cause.

Somatic symptom disorder: persistent body-related symptoms with heavy preoccupation, constant worry about health and frequent visits to doctors. Illness anxiety disorder: persistent preoccupation with the possibility of having or developing a serious illness, with frequent body-checking.

Conversion disorder: reported loss of part or all of some basic body functions (for example, paralysis, blindness, deafness or difficulty walking) with no physical cause, often after a stressful experience and sometimes suddenly.

Dissociation is a severance of the connections between ideas and emotions, involving feelings of unreality, estrangement and sometimes a shift in identity. Dissociative amnesia: extensive but selective memory loss with no known organic cause; dissociative fugue (a part of it) involves unexpected travel away from home and assuming a new identity.

Dissociative identity disorder (once called multiple personality): the person assumes alternate personalities that may or may not be aware of each other. Depersonalisation/derealisation: a dreamlike state where the person feels separated from self and from reality.

ex.q: After a terrifying event, a man cannot remember anything about the week it happened, but medical scans show no brain injury. Which disorder is most likely?
st: Memory loss is selective — focused on a stressful period.
No organic cause is found.
This fits dissociative amnesia.
ex.a: Dissociative amnesia.

topics.rl: Doctors in Indian hospitals often see patients with physical complaints that tests can't explain; a referral to a psychologist or psychiatrist is part of good care, not a dismissal of the patient's suffering.

rv.summary: Somatic symptom disorders turn psychological difficulty into physical symptoms (somatic symptom, illness anxiety, conversion). Dissociative disorders break links between ideas and emotions: amnesia, fugue, dissociative identity disorder and depersonalisation/derealisation.

Matching a case to the disorder
remember: Conversion: loss of a basic body function with no physical cause
Illness anxiety: fear of having a serious illness
Fugue: unexpected travel and new identity
DID: alternate personalities (once multiple personality)
traps: Don't confuse somatic symptom disorder (worry about symptoms) with conversion disorder (loss of function)
Dissociative amnesia has no organic cause

topics.t: Depressive and bipolar disorders; preventing suicide
topics.h: Feeling sad after a bad result is human. Feeling empty, tired and hopeless for weeks, losing interest in everything you used to love — that may be depression, and it deserves care.
p: Major depressive disorder: a period (at least two weeks) of depressed mood and/or loss of interest or pleasure in most activities, along with other symptoms.

Other symptoms include change in body weight, persistent sleep problems, tiredness, inability to think clearly, agitation or greatly slowed behaviour, excessive guilt or worthlessness, and thoughts of death.
Risk factors: genetic make-up, age, gender (women are more likely than men to report depressive disorders), negative life events and lack of social support.

Bipolar I disorder: manic and depressive episodes alternate, sometimes with periods of normal mood in between (once called manic-depressive disorder). Mania involves euphoria, extreme activity, excessive talkativeness, distractibility and poor judgement.

Suicide prevention: warning signs can include talking about wanting to die, withdrawing from friends and activities, sudden mood changes and giving away possessions. Take every sign seriously — listen without judging, stay with the person, tell a trusted adult and connect them to professional help such as Tele-MANAS (14416). Asking someone directly about suicidal thoughts does not put the idea in their head.

ex.q: A person alternates between weeks of extreme energy, non-stop talking and risky spending, and weeks of deep sadness and exhaustion. What disorder does this pattern suggest?
st: High-energy, euphoric, talkative episodes = mania.
Periods of deep sadness = depressive episodes.
Alternating mania and depression = bipolar I disorder.
ex.a: Bipolar I disorder.

topics.rl: Tele-MANAS (dial 14416 or 1-800-891-4416) is India's free, 24×7 mental health helpline in many Indian languages. If you or a friend ever feel hopeless, reaching out is a brave, important first step.

rv.summary: Major depressive disorder is depressed mood or loss of interest for at least two weeks with other symptoms. Bipolar I alternates mania and depression. Suicide warning signs must be taken seriously, with listening and professional help such as Tele-MANAS 14416.

Features of mania and bipolar I
remember: Major depressive disorder: at least two weeks
Bipolar I: alternating manic and depressive episodes
Tele-MANAS: 14416
Asking directly about suicidal thoughts does not put the idea in someone's head
traps: Don't keep a friend's suicidal talk secret
Elation is mania, not depression
Persistent sadness is not laziness

topics.t: Schizophrenia: nature and positive symptoms
topics.h: Imagine hearing voices no one else hears, or being sure strangers are spying on you. For people with schizophrenia these experiences feel completely real.
p: Schizophrenia is a group of psychotic disorders in which personal, social and occupational functioning deteriorate due to disturbed thought processes, strange perceptions, unusual emotional states and motor abnormalities.

Positive symptoms are 'pathological excesses' or bizarre additions. Delusions are false beliefs held firmly on inadequate grounds and not changed by rational argument: persecution (most common — being plotted against or spied on), reference (special personal meaning in others' actions or events), grandeur (being specially empowered or important) and control (feelings, thoughts and actions controlled by others).

Hallucinations are perceptions without external stimuli. Auditory hallucinations (hearing voices) are the most common; others are tactile (tingling, burning), somatic (something happening inside the body), visual, gustatory (taste) and olfactory (smell).

Formal thought disorder: loosening of associations or derailment (rapid shifts between unrelated topics), neologisms (made-up words), perseveration (persistent, inappropriate repetition of the same thoughts) and clang (rhyming words).
Inappropriate affect: emotions unsuited to the situation, such as laughing on hearing sad news.

ex.q: A person insists that a TV news anchor is sending him secret messages meant only for him. Which type of delusion is this?
st: He gives special personal meaning to events (the news broadcast).
That is a delusion of reference.
ex.a: Delusion of reference.

topics.rl: NIMHANS and community programmes like the District Mental Health Programme help people with schizophrenia get medicines, therapy and family support so they can live in their communities.

rv.summary: Schizophrenia is a group of psychotic disorders with deteriorating functioning. Positive symptoms (excesses) include delusions (persecution, reference, grandeur, control), hallucinations (auditory most common), formal thought disorder and inappropriate affect.
focus: Formal thought disorder: derailment, neologisms, perseveration, clang
remember: Delusion: firmly held false belief
Persecution: most common delusion; auditory: most common hallucination
Somatic hallucination: inside the body; tactile: on the skin
Neologism: made-up word
traps: Don't confuse delusions (beliefs) with hallucinations (perceptions)
Somatic is not tactile
Reference means special personal meaning, not grandeur

topics.t: Schizophrenia: negative and psychomotor symptoms, and causes
topics.h: Positive symptoms add something — voices, false beliefs. Negative symptoms take something away — speech, emotion, motivation. Both matter for recovery.
p: Negative symptoms are 'pathological deficits': poverty of speech (alogia — reduced speech and speech content), blunted and flat affect (reduced or no emotional expression), loss of volition (avolition — apathy and inability to start or complete a course of action) and social withdrawal.

Psychomotor symptoms (catatonia): catatonic stupor (motionless and silent for long periods), catatonic rigidity (maintaining a rigid, upright posture for hours) and catatonic posturing (holding awkward, bizarre positions for long periods).
Biological causes: the dopamine hypothesis (excess dopamine activity) and brain structure abnormalities; genetic factors increase risk.

Psychological and socio-cultural causes include family stress, faulty communication patterns and stressful life conditions. In line with the diathesis–stress model, vulnerability and stressors interact.

ex.q: Classify each: (a) hearing voices, (b) speaking very little with almost no content, (c) showing no facial expression even at happy news, (d) standing in one odd position for hours.
st: (a) An excess experience → positive symptom (hallucination).
(b) Reduced speech → negative symptom (alogia).
(c) Reduced emotional expression → negative symptom (flat affect).
(d) Odd motor behaviour → psychomotor symptom (catatonic posturing).
ex.a: (a) Positive, (b) Negative, (c) Negative, (d) Psychomotor.

topics.rl: Rehabilitation programmes in India, such as those at NIMHANS, focus heavily on negative symptoms — helping people rebuild motivation, social skills and daily routines.

rv.summary: Negative symptoms are deficits: alogia, flat affect, avolition and social withdrawal. Psychomotor symptoms include catatonic stupor, rigidity and posturing. Causes include excess dopamine, brain abnormalities, genes and family and life stress.

Biological and psychological causes of schizophrenia
remember: Alogia: poverty of speech; avolition: loss of will; flat affect: reduced emotion

traps: Negative symptoms are deficits, not excesses

topics.t: Neurodevelopmental disorders
topics.h: A brilliant child who struggles to read the board, another who can't sit still, a third who lines up toys perfectly but avoids eye contact — each may need a different kind of support.
p: Neurodevelopmental disorders first appear in early development and affect functioning in daily life, school and relationships.

Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) has two main features: inattention (difficulty sustaining attention, easily distracted, not following instructions) and hyperactivity–impulsivity (difficulty waiting or resisting urges, blurting answers, constant motion, fidgeting).

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD): varying degrees of difficulty in social interaction and communication, with restricted interests and a strong need for routine and repetitive behaviours (such as rocking).

Intellectual disability: below-average intellectual functioning (IQ of about 70 or below) together with deficits in adaptive behaviour (communication, self-care, social skills, home living), manifested before 18.

Specific learning disorder: difficulty in perceiving or processing information efficiently and accurately, seen in reading, writing or maths skills well below the expected level for the child's age, starting in the early school years.

ex.q: A 7-year-old with average intelligence reads far below grade level, mixes up letters and struggles with spelling despite good teaching. Which disorder is most likely?
st: Intelligence is average, so intellectual disability is unlikely.
The difficulty is specific to reading and spelling.
This fits specific learning disorder.
ex.a: Specific learning disorder.

topics.rl: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 recognises specific learning disabilities and autism spectrum disorder, and CBSE allows accommodations such as extra time and scribes for eligible students.

rv.summary: Neurodevelopmental disorders appear early in development: ADHD (inattention, hyperactivity–impulsivity), autism spectrum disorder (social-communication difficulty with repetitive behaviour), intellectual disability and specific learning disorder.

ASD: social and communication difficulty, restricted interests, need for routine
Intellectual disability: IQ about 70 or below + adaptive deficits before 18
SLD: specific academic skill difficulty

topics.t: Disruptive, conduct and feeding–eating disorders
topics.h: One teen argues with every adult rule. Another hurts animals and steals. A third sees herself as overweight when she's dangerously thin. Very different problems, all needing understanding and help.
p: Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD): age-inappropriate amounts of stubbornness, irritability, defiance, disobedience and hostility. Unlike conduct disorder, it does not typically involve aggression towards people or animals or destruction of property.

Conduct disorder: age-inappropriate actions and attitudes that violate family expectations, social norms and the personal or property rights of others — aggression towards people or animals, property damage, deceitfulness, theft and serious rule-breaking.
Types of aggressive behaviour: verbal (name-calling, swearing), physical (hitting, fighting), hostile (aimed at injuring others) and proactive (dominating and bullying without provocation).

Anorexia nervosa: a distorted body image — seeing oneself as overweight — with refusal to eat, compulsive exercise and unusual eating habits, leading to dangerous weight loss. Bulimia nervosa: eating excessive amounts followed by purging, with feelings of shame afterwards.

Binge eating disorder: frequent episodes of out-of-control eating, often faster than usual and until uncomfortably full, without purging. Eating disorders are serious but treatable; early help matters.

ex.q: Compare: Riya (body weight very low, believes she is fat, refuses meals) and Simran (normal weight, eats large amounts secretly then purges, feels ashamed).
st: Riya: distorted body image, food refusal, very low weight → anorexia nervosa.
Simran: binge eating followed by purging → bulimia nervosa.
Key difference: anorexia involves restriction and very low weight; bulimia involves binge–purge cycles.
ex.a: Riya: anorexia nervosa; Simran: bulimia nervosa.

topics.rl: Indian teens face heavy pressure from social media 'body goals'. School counsellors now watch for signs of eating disorders and encourage early, non-judgemental support.

rv.summary: ODD involves defiance and hostility; conduct disorder involves violating others' rights through aggression, theft and damage. Eating disorders are anorexia nervosa (distorted body image, food refusal), bulimia nervosa (binge and purge) and binge eating disorder (no purging).

Bulimia: binge + purge; binge eating disorder: binge without purging

topics.t: Substance-related and addictive disorders
topics.h: 'Just once won't hurt.' But some substances change the brain so that 'once' turns into 'need'. Understanding tolerance and withdrawal explains why addiction is so hard to escape.
p: Substance use disorders include substance dependence (intense craving with tolerance and withdrawal) and substance abuse (recurrent use with significant harmful consequences). Tolerance: needing more of a substance to get the same effect. Withdrawal: unpleasant physical and psychological symptoms when use stops or reduces.

Alcohol: regular heavy drinkers come to rely on alcohol to face difficult situations; it eventually harms family and social relationships, ability to think and work, and physical health (such as liver damage). Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant.

Heroin (an opioid): use quickly interferes with social and occupational functioning; most users develop dependence with tolerance and withdrawal. Overdose can dangerously slow breathing and can be fatal.

Cocaine (a stimulant): regular use can lead to abuse, poor functioning in relationships and work, and problems with short-term memory and attention. Withdrawal brings depression, fatigue, sleep problems, irritability and anxiety.
Help is available: de-addiction centres, counselling and helplines. The national toll-free de-addiction helpline is 14446, and Tele-MANAS (14416) can also guide people.

ex.q: Vikas once felt relaxed after one drink; now he needs four drinks for the same effect, and when he stops he feels shaky, anxious and sweaty. Which two features of dependence are shown?
st: Needing more for the same effect = tolerance.
Shakiness, anxiety and sweating on stopping = withdrawal.
ex.a: Tolerance and withdrawal.

topics.rl: The Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan runs awareness drives in schools and colleges, and the national de-addiction helpline (14446) connects people to counselling and treatment.

rv.summary: Substance use disorders include dependence (craving, tolerance, withdrawal) and abuse (recurrent harmful use). Alcohol is a CNS depressant, heroin an opioid and cocaine a stimulant. Help is available through de-addiction centres and helplines (14446, Tele-MANAS 14416).

topics.t: Nature, characteristics and goals of psychotherapy
topics.h: Talking to a friend helps. So why train for years to become a therapist? Because psychotherapy is a systematic, theory-based process — not just a chat.
p: Psychotherapy is a voluntary relationship between the one seeking treatment (the client) and the one who treats (the therapist). Its purpose is to help the client solve psychological problems.

Characteristics: (1) systematic application of principles from theories of therapy; (2) only trained persons with practical, supervised experience practise it; (3) the therapeutic situation involves a therapist and a client who seeks help; (4) the relationship is confidential, interpersonal and dynamic.
Goals (part 1): reinforcing the client's resolve for betterment; lessening emotional pressure; unfolding the potential for positive growth; modifying habits.

Goals (part 2): changing thinking patterns; increasing self-awareness; improving interpersonal relations and communication; facilitating decision-making; becoming aware of one's choices in life; relating to one's social environment in a more creative and self-aware manner.

ex.q: A friend says, 'Therapy is just talking — my uncle gives great advice too.' Give two characteristics that make psychotherapy different.
st: It applies principles from established theories systematically.
Only trained, supervised professionals practise it.
It is a confidential, professional relationship focused on the client's goals.
ex.a: Psychotherapy is theory-based, systematic, done by trained professionals and confidential — unlike casual advice.

topics.rl: India's Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) registers clinical psychologists, ensuring that people offering therapy have proper training and supervision.

rv.summary: Psychotherapy is a voluntary, confidential relationship between a client and a trained therapist that systematically applies theory to solve psychological problems. Its goals include lessening emotional pressure, modifying habits, changing thinking and increasing self-awareness.

topics.t: The therapeutic relationship
topics.h: 'I feel sorry for you' versus 'I can feel what this is like for you.' One is sympathy, the other empathy — and therapists need the second.
p: The therapeutic relationship (alliance) has two major components. It is contractual: two willing individuals enter a partnership to help the client overcome problems. It is of limited duration: it lasts until the client can deal with problems and take control of life.
The client must be able to trust the therapist; what the client shares is kept confidential, and the therapist must not exploit this trust.
The therapist shows unconditional positive regard (warmth and acceptance regardless of what the client says) and empathy for the client.

Empathy: understanding the client's situation from the client's perspective, as if one were in their place. Sympathy: compassion and pity for another's suffering, but without feeling what they feel. Intellectual understanding: cold — one understands the facts but feels neither.
The relationship must remain professional, with clear boundaries.

ex.q: A client says she feels like a failure after losing her job. Write one empathic, one sympathetic and one intellectual response.
st: Empathic: 'It sounds like losing the job has shaken your sense of worth; that must feel heavy.'
Sympathetic: 'Oh, poor you, that's so sad.'
Intellectual: 'Job losses are common in this economy.'
ex.a: Only the first truly enters the client's perspective — empathy.

topics.rl: Indian therapy guidelines stress confidentiality and boundaries — a therapist may not, for instance, start a business partnership with a client, because it would compromise the professional relationship.

rv.summary: The therapeutic alliance is contractual and of limited duration. It rests on trust and confidentiality, with the therapist offering unconditional positive regard and empathy within professional boundaries.

topics.t: Types of therapies and bases of classification
topics.h: If two therapists treat the same anxious client, one might teach relaxation and another explore the meaning of the client's life. How do we compare such different approaches?
p: Psychotherapies fall into three broad groups: psychodynamic, behaviour and existential (humanistic-existential) therapies. Historically, psychodynamic therapy emerged first, then behaviour therapy; existential therapies, called the 'third force', emerged last. (Details of psychodynamic therapy are not part of the rationalised syllabus.)

Therapies are compared on six parameters: (1) what is the cause of the problem, (2) how did the cause come into existence, (3) what is the chief method of treatment, (4) what is the nature of the therapeutic relationship, (5) what is the chief benefit to the client, (6) what is the duration of treatment.

For example, behaviour therapy sees the cause as faulty learning, uses behavioural techniques, and usually runs for a few months; humanistic-existential therapy sees the cause as lack of meaning and alienation, and aims at personal growth.

ex.q: Use the six parameters to describe behaviour therapy for a child's fear of dogs.
st: Cause: a learned fear response.
How it arose: faulty conditioning, e.g. after a dog chased the child.
Method: behavioural techniques such as systematic desensitisation.
Relationship: therapist guides and trains the client.
Benefit: fear reduced, normal behaviour restored.
Duration: usually a few months.
ex.a: Each parameter can be answered, allowing comparison with other therapies.

topics.rl: Just as a doctor compares medicines by cause, method, side effects and duration, NCERT compares therapies on six parameters — a handy table for board answers.

rv.summary: Psychotherapies fall into psychodynamic, behaviour and existential (third force) groups, emerging in that order. They are compared on six parameters: cause, how it arose, chief method, relationship, chief benefit and duration.

topics.t: Behaviour therapy: principles and behavioural analysis
topics.h: A child throws a tantrum at dinner every night. A behaviour therapist doesn't ask about his dreams — she asks: what happens just before, and just after?
p: Behaviour therapies hold that psychological distress arises from faulty behaviour or thought patterns learned in the past. The focus is on the client's present behaviours; the past matters only to understand how the faulty pattern began.

Behavioural analysis identifies malfunctioning behaviours, the faulty learning behind them, the antecedent factors (what triggers them) and the maintaining factors (what keeps them going). It looks at antecedents, the maladaptive behaviour and its consequences.

Antecedent operations control behaviour by changing something that precedes it. An establishing operation increases or decreases the reinforcing value of a consequence; for example, if a child fusses at dinner, giving him less food at tea-time makes him hungrier at dinner, increasing the value of dinner and reducing fussing.
Consequent operations change the consequences that follow a behaviour (rewarding wanted behaviour, not rewarding unwanted behaviour).
Relaxation procedures reduce arousal; once the client is calm, behavioural techniques can be applied more effectively.

ex.q: Analyse Aryan's tantrums: they start when his favourite cartoon is switched off for homework (A), he screams (B), and his parents switch the TV back on (C). What keeps the tantrum going?
st: Antecedent: TV switched off.
Behaviour: screaming tantrum.
Consequence: TV switched back on — this rewards the tantrum.
The consequence is the maintaining factor.
ex.a: The reward of getting the TV back maintains the tantrums.

topics.rl: Parents in many Indian homes unknowingly reward tantrums by giving in. Behaviour therapists teach them to change the consequence — a simple shift with big results.

rv.summary: Behaviour therapy treats distress as learned faulty behaviour, focusing on the present. Behavioural analysis identifies antecedents, the behaviour and maintaining consequences, and uses antecedent operations (like establishing operations), consequent operations and relaxation.

Antecedent operation: change what comes before the behaviour
Establishing operation: changes the reinforcing value of a consequence
traps: Behaviour therapy focuses on the present, not dreams or the deep past

topics.t: Reinforcement, aversive conditioning and token economy
topics.h: Stars on a chart, a favourite dish after homework, ignoring a sulk — these everyday tricks are real behaviour therapy techniques.
p: Negative reinforcement (as NCERT describes it): an undesired response is followed by an outcome that is painful or not liked, so the person learns the response that avoids it — for example, going out in winter without woollens brings the cold, so one teaches oneself to wear woollen clothes.

Aversive conditioning: repeated association of an undesired response with an aversive (unpleasant) consequence, so the behaviour becomes unpleasant and decreases. For example, in treatment for alcohol dependence, the smell of alcohol is repeatedly paired with a mild unpleasant stimulus under professional supervision.
Positive reinforcement: if an adaptive behaviour occurs rarely, it is followed by a reward (for example, a favourite dish when homework is done regularly).
Token economy: a person earns a token each time a wanted behaviour occurs; tokens are collected and exchanged for a reward such as an outing or a treat.

Differential reinforcement: increasing wanted behaviour and reducing unwanted behaviour at the same time — either by positively reinforcing the wanted behaviour and following the unwanted one with a disliked outcome (negative reinforcement, in NCERT's terms), or, less painfully, by reinforcing the wanted behaviour and ignoring the unwanted one (e.g., parents take a girl to the film when she doesn't sulk, and ignore her when she sulks).

ex.q: Design a token economy for residents of a rehabilitation centre who rarely make their beds.
st: Target behaviour: making the bed every morning.
Each time it is done, give one token.
Tokens can be exchanged, e.g. 10 tokens for an outing or a special treat.
Gradually, the behaviour increases because it is reinforced.
ex.a: Tokens are given for each instance of the wanted behaviour and exchanged for rewards.

topics.rl: Many Indian schools use house points or star charts for punctuality and cleanliness — a classroom version of the token economy.

rv.summary: Behavioural techniques include positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement (as NCERT describes it), aversive conditioning, token economy and differential reinforcement, which increases wanted behaviour while reducing unwanted behaviour.

topics.t: Systematic desensitisation and modelling
topics.h: Scared of heights? A therapist won't push you off a cliff. She'll start with a picture of a stool — while you're deeply relaxed — and climb slowly from there.
p: Systematic desensitisation, introduced by Joseph Wolpe, treats phobias and irrational fears.

Steps: (1) the client is interviewed to identify fear-provoking situations; (2) together they build a hierarchy of anxiety-provoking stimuli, with the least anxiety-provoking at the bottom; (3) the client is relaxed; (4) the client imagines the least anxiety-provoking situation and stops if any tension is felt; (5) over sessions, the client moves up the hierarchy while staying relaxed.

It works on the principle of reciprocal inhibition: two mutually opposing forces (relaxation and anxiety) cannot exist at the same time; the stronger relaxation response inhibits the weaker anxiety response.

Modelling: the client learns to behave in a certain way by observing a role model. Vicarious learning means learning by observing others being reinforced. The therapist may act as the model and reinforce small changes towards the desired behaviour.

ex.q: Build a hierarchy for Ritu, who fears dogs, from least to most anxiety-provoking: touching a dog, seeing a picture of a dog, a dog in the next room, a dog across the street.
st: Least: seeing a picture.
Next: a dog across the street.
Next: a dog in the next room.
Most: touching a dog.
She moves up only while staying relaxed.
ex.a: Picture → dog across the street → dog in next room → touching a dog.

topics.rl: Fear of flying is common among first-time flyers in India. Therapists use desensitisation — videos of airports, then sitting in a parked plane — before an actual flight.

rv.summary: Wolpe's systematic desensitisation treats phobias by building an anxiety hierarchy and pairing relaxation with each step from least to most feared, using reciprocal inhibition. Modelling teaches behaviour through observing a role model (vicarious learning).

remember: Systematic desensitisation: Joseph Wolpe
Hierarchy: least anxiety at the bottom
Reciprocal inhibition: relaxation and anxiety cannot coexist
Vicarious learning: learning by observing others being reinforced
traps: Start with the least, not the most, feared situation
If tension appears, stop and relax; don't push through
Modelling is observation-based, not aversive

topics.t: Cognitive therapy: Ellis's Rational Emotive Therapy
topics.h: A friend doesn't reply to your message. You feel hurt. But was it the unanswered message — or your belief 'She must hate me' — that hurt?
p: Cognitive therapies locate the cause of psychological distress in irrational thoughts and beliefs.

Albert Ellis's Rational Emotive Therapy (RET): irrational beliefs mediate between antecedent events and their consequences. ABC model: A = antecedent event, B = belief, C = consequence (emotions and behaviour).
The first step is the ABC analysis: identify the antecedent events that caused distress and the irrational beliefs behind them, through client interviews.

Irrational beliefs are marked by 'musts' and 'shoulds' (e.g., 'I must be loved by everyone', 'I should never fail'), and by awfulising. They distort how the antecedent event is perceived, producing negative emotions and behaviours.

The therapist refutes irrational beliefs through non-directive questioning that is gentle, without probing or being directive, making the client think deeper about their assumptions and gradually adopt rational beliefs.

ex.q: Apply the ABC model: Kunal scores 70% in a test (A), believes 'I must always score above 90% or I'm worthless' (B), and feels hopeless and stops studying (C).
st: A (antecedent): 70% in the test.
B (belief): an irrational 'must' — 'I must always score above 90%.'
C (consequence): hopelessness and avoidance.
Therapy targets B, not A: replace it with 'I'd like higher marks, but 70% doesn't make me worthless.'
ex.a: A = 70% score; B = irrational 'must' belief; C = hopelessness — change B to change C.

topics.rl: Coaching-centre students in Kota often carry beliefs like 'I must crack the exam this year or my life is over'. Counsellors use RET-style questioning to soften these musts.

rv.summary: Ellis's Rational Emotive Therapy holds that irrational beliefs (B) mediate between antecedent events (A) and consequences (C). Therapy starts with ABC analysis and gently questions 'must' and 'should' beliefs until rational beliefs replace them.
remember: RET: Albert Ellis
A = antecedent, B = belief, C = consequence
Irrational beliefs: 'musts' and 'shoulds', awfulising
Non-directive, gentle questioning
traps: Events do not cause consequences directly; beliefs mediate
RET targets B, not A
RET is not Beck's therapy

topics.t: Beck's cognitive therapy and CBT
topics.h: 'Nobody likes me.' 'I'm stupid.' Thoughts that pop up automatically can feel like facts. Aaron Beck taught people to question them.
p: Aaron Beck: childhood experiences provide basic cognitive schemas or core beliefs (e.g., 'I am unwanted'). Critical incidents later in life activate these core schemas.

Activated core schemas produce negative automatic thoughts — persistent irrational thoughts such as 'Nobody loves me', 'I am ugly', 'I am stupid'. Cognitive distortions are ways of thinking that distort reality in a negative way; repeated, they lead to anxiety and depression.

Therapy uses gentle, non-threatening disputation of beliefs and thoughts through Socratic questioning, such as 'Why should everyone love you?' or 'What does it mean to you to succeed?' The client discovers contradictions in their own thinking and changes their views.

Cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) is a short, effective therapy for many disorders such as anxiety, depression and panic attacks. It combines cognitive therapy with behavioural techniques and follows a biopsychosocial approach — relaxation for the biological, cognitive and behavioural methods for the psychological, and environmental changes for the social.

ex.q: Riddhi was often told as a child that she was a burden (core schema: 'I am unwanted'). Years later, a friend cancels plans and she thinks 'Nobody wants me around.' Identify each part using Beck's model.
st: Childhood experience → core schema 'I am unwanted'.
Critical incident: friend cancels plans.
Activated schema produces a negative automatic thought: 'Nobody wants me around.'
A therapist would use Socratic questions: 'What other reasons might she have had to cancel?'
ex.a: Core schema → critical incident → negative automatic thought, challenged by Socratic questioning.

topics.rl: CBT is now offered in many Indian hospitals and through digital platforms; NIMHANS has trained counsellors to deliver CBT-based support for depression and anxiety.

rv.summary: Beck's cognitive therapy holds that childhood experiences form core schemas, which critical incidents activate, producing negative automatic thoughts and distortions. Socratic questioning disputes them. CBT combines cognitive and behavioural methods in a biopsychosocial approach.
focus: Core schemas, critical incidents and negative automatic thoughts
remember: Beck: childhood experiences → core schemas; critical incidents activate them → negative automatic thoughts
Socratic questioning: gentle, non-threatening
CBT: short, effective for anxiety, depression, panic attacks
traps: Core schemas form in childhood, not adulthood
Critical incidents activate schemas; they do not create them
Beck uses Socratic questioning, not free association

topics.t: Humanistic-existential therapies: logotherapy, client-centred and Gestalt
topics.h: Victor Frankl survived a Nazi concentration camp and came out with a powerful idea: people can endure almost anything if they find meaning in it.
p: Humanistic-existential therapies see psychological distress as arising from loneliness, alienation and an inability to find meaning and fulfilment. People have an innate need for personal growth and self-actualisation. The therapist provides a permissive, non-judgemental, accepting atmosphere and acts as a facilitator; the client is responsible for the success of therapy.

Logotherapy (Victor Frankl): 'logos' means soul, so logotherapy is 'treatment of the soul'. It helps clients find meaning even in painful experiences (meaning-making). Existential anxiety is neurotic anxiety of spiritual origin, arising from problems about the meaning of life. Paradoxical intention encourages clients to deliberately wish for or do the very thing they fear, often with humour, to weaken anxiety.

Client-centred therapy (Carl Rogers): the therapist shows empathy, warmth and unconditional positive regard, and uses reflection of feelings and clarification of the client's thoughts. It is non-directive, helping clients reconnect with their feelings and grow.

Gestalt therapy (Frederick 'Fritz' Perls with Laura Perls): 'gestalt' means whole. Its goal is to increase self-awareness and self-acceptance; clients learn to recognise bodily processes and emotions blocked from awareness, and may act out fantasies about feelings and conflicts. It can be used in groups.

ex.q: A client says, 'I feel nobody at home understands me.' What would a client-centred therapist say?
st: Reflect the feeling back without judging or advising.
'You're feeling lonely and unheard by your family.'
This shows empathy and lets the client explore further.
ex.a: A reflection such as 'You feel lonely and unheard at home' — showing empathy and acceptance.

topics.rl: Meaning-centred counselling inspired by logotherapy is used with patients facing serious illness in palliative care centres, helping them find purpose in family, relationships and helping others.

rv.summary: Humanistic-existential therapies treat distress from alienation and lack of meaning. Frankl's logotherapy helps find meaning (paradoxical intention), Rogers' client-centred therapy uses empathy, warmth and reflection, and Perls' Gestalt therapy builds self-awareness and self-acceptance.
focus: Causes of distress in humanistic-existential therapy
Logotherapy: meaning-making, existential anxiety, paradoxical intention
remember: Logotherapy: Victor Frankl; logos = soul
Paradoxical intention: deliberately wish for or do what one fears
Client-centred (Rogers): reflection, clarification, unconditional positive regard
Gestalt (Fritz and Laura Perls): self-awareness, self-acceptance
traps: Logos means soul, not logic
Reflection of feelings belongs to client-centred, not Gestalt, therapy

topics.t: Alternative therapies: yoga and meditation
topics.h: International Yoga Day draws millions every 21 June. Beyond flexibility, research at Indian institutes shows breathing-based yoga can help with depression.
p: Alternative therapies are alternatives to conventional drug treatment or psychotherapy — for example, yoga, meditation, acupuncture and herbal remedies. They are often used alongside, not instead of, professional treatment.
Yoga is an ancient Indian technique described in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras. As therapy it may use asanas (body postures), pranayama (breathing practices) or both.

Sudarshan Kriya Yoga (SKY) uses rapid breathing techniques to induce hyperventilation. Research at NIMHANS, Bengaluru, found SKY beneficial for depression; it is a low-risk, low-cost adjunct for stress, anxiety, PTSD, stress-related illnesses and substance abuse.

Meditation focuses attention on the breath or an object, thought or mantra. In vipassana (mindfulness-based) meditation there is no fixed object; the person passively observes bodily sensations and thoughts as they arise. Kundalini yoga, which combines breathing with chanting of mantras, has also been found useful for mental disorders.
Benefits include better mood, attention, mental focus, stress tolerance and overall well-being. People should learn these practices from trained teachers and continue medical care when needed.

ex.q: Distinguish focused meditation from vipassana meditation.
st: Focused meditation: attention is fixed on one object, such as the breath or a mantra.
Vipassana (mindfulness-based): no fixed object; one passively observes sensations and thoughts as they come and go.
ex.a: Focused meditation fixes attention on one object; vipassana observes everything passively without a fixed object.

topics.rl: NIMHANS in Bengaluru has an integrated yoga programme, and many Indian hospitals now offer yoga as an add-on to standard treatment for depression and anxiety.

rv.summary: Alternative therapies like yoga and meditation are used alongside conventional treatment. Yoga uses asanas and pranayama; SKY (rapid breathing) helps depression; focused meditation fixes attention, vipassana observes passively, and Kundalini combines breathing with mantras.
focus: Focused vs vipassana meditation; Kundalini yoga
remember: Pranayama: breathing; asanas: postures
SKY: rapid breathing, hyperventilation; NIMHANS found it helps depression
Vipassana: no fixed object, passive observation
Kundalini: breathing + mantra chanting
