topics.t: Factors that heal and ethics in psychotherapy
topics.h: Two clients get the same therapy; one improves fast, the other slowly. Healing depends on more than technique — and the therapist must follow strict ethics.
p: Factors contributing to healing: (1) the techniques used by the therapist; (2) the therapeutic alliance — the therapist's regular availability, warmth and empathy; (3) catharsis — emotional unburdening or release, often in early sessions.

(4) Non-specific factors: patient variables (motivation for change, expectation of improvement) and therapist variables (positive nature, absence of unresolved emotional conflicts, good mental health).

Ethics in psychotherapy: informed consent; confidentiality of the client; alleviating personal distress; integrity of the practitioner–client relationship; respect for human rights and dignity; professional competence and skills.
Informed consent means the client is told about the nature, purpose and possible effects of therapy and agrees voluntarily.

ex.q: In her first session, Asha cries for a long time while describing her problems and later says she feels 'lighter'. Which healing factor is this?
st: Emotional release while expressing problems.
This unburdening is catharsis.
ex.a: Catharsis.

topics.rl: India's Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 gives people the right to confidentiality and to informed consent for treatment — the same ethical principles therapists follow.

rv.summary: Healing comes from the therapist's techniques, the therapeutic alliance, catharsis and non-specific patient and therapist variables. Ethics require informed consent, confidentiality, relief of distress, integrity, respect for rights and dignity, and competence.
remember: Catharsis: emotional unburdening
Patient variables: motivation, expectation of improvement
Therapist variables: positive nature, no unresolved conflicts, good mental health
Informed consent: told and agrees voluntarily
traps: Motivation is a patient variable, not a therapist variable
Disguised stories that identify a client still break confidentiality
Catharsis is not transference

topics.t: Rehabilitation of the mentally ill
topics.h: Medicines may quieten the voices, but what about getting a job, making friends and planning a day? That's where rehabilitation comes in.
p: Treatment has two parts: reducing symptoms, and improving the person's level of functioning and quality of life. Rehabilitation aims to empower the patient to become a productive member of society to the greatest extent possible.
Many patients, especially with schizophrenia, have negative symptoms such as lack of interest and motivation; rehabilitation addresses these.

Occupational therapy: patients are taught skills such as candle-making, paper-bag making and weaving to help form a work discipline. Social skills training: interpersonal skills are developed through role play, imitation and instruction, so patients learn to function in social groups.
Cognitive retraining: improves basic cognitive functions such as attention, memory and executive functions.
Vocational training: once the patient has improved sufficiently, they gain skills needed for productive employment.

ex.q: Plan rehabilitation for Raju, a young man recovering from schizophrenia who forgets instructions, avoids people and has never worked.
st: Cognitive retraining for attention and memory problems.
Social skills training using role play to build interaction.
Occupational therapy (e.g. candle-making) to build work discipline.
Vocational training for a job once he is ready.
ex.a: Cognitive retraining, social skills training, occupational therapy, then vocational training.

topics.rl: Centres like NIMHANS run day-care and vocational rehabilitation, and some Indian NGOs help recovering patients run small businesses such as tailoring units and cafés.

rv.summary: Rehabilitation goes beyond reducing symptoms to improve functioning and quality of life, especially for negative symptoms. It uses occupational therapy, social skills training, cognitive retraining and, once improved, vocational training.
focus: The four rehabilitation methods and their targets
remember: Occupational therapy: candle-making, weaving for work discipline
Social skills training: role play, imitation, instruction
Cognitive retraining: attention, memory, executive functions

traps: Don't confuse occupational therapy (work discipline) with vocational training (job skills)

topics.t: Social psychology and the building blocks of social behaviour
topics.h: Why do you clap louder when the whole stadium claps? Why do you trust some news channels and not others? Social psychology studies how others shape what we think, feel and do.
p: Social psychology is the branch of psychology that investigates how the behaviour of individuals is affected by others and by the social environment — how we think, feel and act in social situations.
In the rationalised CBSE syllabus, this chapter focuses on attitudes (their nature, formation and change, and the attitude–behaviour link) and on prejudice and discrimination.
Social behaviour is shaped by social cognition — the mental processes of gathering and interpreting information about the social world — and by social influence from others.
Attitudes, beliefs and values are the building blocks of social behaviour: they shape how we judge people, events and ideas, and how we act towards them.

ex.q: Riya decides to stop using plastic bags after her friends start a 'no plastic' drive. Which aspects of social behaviour are involved?
st: She gathers and interprets information about the drive — social cognition.
Her friends' behaviour affects her — social influence.
A new attitude towards plastic is forming — a building block of social behaviour.
ex.a: Social cognition, social influence and attitude formation.

topics.rl: When neighbours in an Indian housing society all start segregating waste, newcomers quickly do the same — social psychology in action.

rv.summary: Social psychology studies how others and the social environment affect individual behaviour. Social behaviour is shaped by social cognition and social influence, with attitudes, beliefs and values as its building blocks.
focus: Attitudes, beliefs and values as building blocks
remember: Social psychology: how individual behaviour is affected by others and the social environment
Social cognition: gathering and interpreting information about the social world
Building blocks: attitudes, beliefs, values
traps: Social cognition is not social facilitation
Social psychology is about people in social settings, not brain chemistry alone

topics.t: Nature of attitudes and their A-B-C components
topics.h: 'I love cricket' (feeling), 'I think cricket builds teamwork' (thought), 'I play every evening' (action). Three sentences, one attitude.
p: An attitude is a state of the mind — a set of views or thoughts regarding a topic (the attitude object) — that has an evaluative feature (positive, negative or neutral).

The tri-component (A-B-C) model: Affective component — the emotional part (feelings). Behavioural (conative) component — the tendency to act in a certain way. Cognitive component — the thought or belief part.
Attitude objects can be people, groups, objects, ideas or issues (e.g., attitude towards online classes, towards saving water).
Attitudes are fairly stable and help guide behaviour, though they can change.

ex.q: Identify the A, B and C components: 'I believe planting trees reduces pollution. I feel happy seeing green parks. I plant a sapling every monsoon.'
st: 'I believe planting trees reduces pollution' → cognitive.
'I feel happy seeing green parks' → affective.
'I plant a sapling every monsoon' → behavioural (conative).
ex.a: Cognitive, affective and behavioural components respectively.

topics.rl: The 'Swachh' cleanliness drives in many Indian cities try to work on all three components: information (cognitive), pride in a clean city (affective) and actual clean-ups (behavioural).

rv.summary: An attitude is a state of mind about an attitude object with an evaluative feature. Its A-B-C (tri-component) model has an affective (feeling), behavioural or conative (action) and cognitive (belief) component.
focus: Identifying A, B and C components in statements
remember: Affective: feelings
Behavioural (conative): tendency to act
Cognitive: thoughts and beliefs
A-B-C = tri-component model
traps: 'Conative' means behavioural, not cognitive
'I think...' is cognitive, not affective

topics.t: Beliefs, values and features of attitudes
topics.h: Rate your view on space exploration from 1 (very negative) to 5 (very positive). Your number reveals two features of your attitude: its valence and how extreme it is.
p: Beliefs are the cognitive component of attitudes and form the ground on which attitudes stand (for example, belief in democracy). Values are attitudes or beliefs that contain a 'should' or 'ought' aspect, such as moral values like honesty and hard work. Values form when a belief or attitude becomes an inseparable part of one's outlook on life, so they are hard to change.
Valence (positivity or negativity): on a 5-point scale (1 = very negative, 2 = negative, 3 = neutral, 4 = positive, 5 = very positive), a rating of 4 shows positive valence.
Extremeness: how positive or negative the attitude is. Ratings 1 and 5 are equally extreme and are more extreme than 2 and 4; a rating of 3 is the least extreme.

Simplicity or complexity (multiplexity): how many attitudes there are within a broader attitude. An attitude towards health and well-being, for example, includes many smaller attitudes (physical health, happiness, diet) — it is complex.
Centrality: the role of a particular attitude in the attitude system. A central attitude influences many other attitudes and is more resistant to change than peripheral ones.

ex.q: Arjun rates his view of nuclear energy as 2, and Leena rates hers as 5 on a 1–5 scale. Compare valence and extremeness.
st: Arjun: 2 → negative valence.
Leena: 5 → positive valence.
Extremeness: 5 is at the end of the scale; 2 is one step from neutral.
Leena's attitude is more extreme.
ex.a: Arjun's attitude is negative, Leena's is positive and more extreme.

topics.rl: Survey agencies in India ask voters and consumers to rate views on 5-point scales — the numbers capture valence and extremeness of attitudes towards products and policies.

rv.summary: Beliefs are the cognitive base of attitudes; values add a 'should' aspect and resist change. Attitudes differ in valence, extremeness, simplicity or complexity, and centrality.

Simple vs complex and central vs peripheral attitudes
remember: Valence: positive or negative
Extremeness: 1 and 5 most extreme, 3 least
Complex (multiplex): many attitudes within one
Central: influences many others, resists change
traps: 1 and 5 are equally extreme, though of opposite valence
3 is neutral, the least extreme

topics.t: How attitudes are formed
topics.h: Why do you like a subject? Often it started with a teacher you liked. Attitudes are learned — and there are five main ways it happens.
p: Learning through association: a positive attitude towards one thing spreads to what it is linked with (e.g., liking a teacher leads to liking the subject she teaches).
Learning through rewards and punishment: being praised for a behaviour builds a positive attitude towards it (e.g., praised for doing yoga → positive attitude to yoga).
Learning through modelling (observation): watching others being praised or punished for holding an attitude or behaving in a certain way.

Learning through group or cultural norms: norms are unwritten rules about behaviour expected in a group or culture; over time they become part of our attitudes. Learning through exposure to information: books, the media and biographies of admired people shape attitudes.

Factors in attitude formation: family and school environment (especially in early years), reference groups (groups whose norms one accepts), personal experiences, and media-related influences (print, TV, internet — which can create both positive and negative attitudes).

ex.q: Ishita sees her elder brother praised by the family for volunteering at a blood donation camp, and she develops a positive attitude towards volunteering. Which process is this?
st: She did not volunteer herself or get rewarded directly.
She watched someone else being praised.
Learning by observing others = modelling.
ex.a: Learning through modelling (observation).

topics.rl: Biographies of people like Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam have inspired positive attitudes towards science in many Indian students — an example of learning through exposure to information.

rv.summary: Attitudes are learned through association, rewards and punishment, modelling, group or cultural norms and exposure to information. Factors include family and school, reference groups, personal experiences and the media.

Matching a case to the process
remember: Association: liking spreads to what is linked
Modelling: observing others rewarded or punished

topics.t: Attitude change: Heider's balance and Festinger's dissonance
topics.h: You know junk food is unhealthy, yet you eat it every day. That uneasy feeling? Festinger called it cognitive dissonance — and it pushes you to change something.
p: Heider's balance concept is expressed as a P-O-X triangle: P is the person whose attitude is studied, O is another person, and X is the attitude object. Each of the three relations (P–O, P–X, O–X) can be positive or negative.

Imbalance exists when all three sides are negative, or when two sides are positive and one is negative. Balance exists when all three are positive, or when two are negative and one is positive. (Tip: multiply the signs — a positive product means balance.)
Imbalance is uncomfortable, so the attitude changes in the direction of balance.

Festinger's cognitive dissonance: the cognitive components of an attitude must be consistent (consonant). If two cognitions are dissonant (e.g., 'Junk food harms health' and 'I eat junk food daily'), one of them is changed to restore consonance (e.g., 'I'll eat junk food only once a week').
Both balance and dissonance are examples of cognitive consistency: two components or elements of an attitude must be consistent with each other.

ex.q: P (Priya) likes O (Omar), Priya likes cricket (X), but Omar dislikes cricket. Is this balanced? How might it change?
st: P–O positive (+), P–X positive (+), O–X negative (−).
Two positive and one negative → product is negative → imbalance.
To restore balance, Priya may start liking cricket less, or persuade Omar to like it, or like Omar less.
ex.a: Imbalanced; one relation must change to restore balance.

topics.rl: Anti-smoking ads in Indian cinemas create dissonance — 'Smoking kills' versus 'I smoke' — hoping viewers will resolve it by quitting.

rv.summary: Heider's balance theory uses the P-O-X triangle: imbalance (all negative, or two positive and one negative) pushes attitudes towards balance. Festinger's cognitive dissonance says inconsistent cognitions make one change. Both reflect cognitive consistency.

Cognitive dissonance and how it is reduced
remember: P: person; O: other person; X: attitude object
Positive product of signs = balance; negative = imbalance

traps: Two negatives and one positive is balanced, not imbalanced
Don't credit dissonance to Heider

topics.t: Mohsin's two-step concept and features of the existing attitude
topics.h: Your favourite cricketer starts eating millets and posts about it. A month later, you're trying ragi dosa. An Indian psychologist explained this in two neat steps.
p: S.M. Mohsin's two-step concept: the target is the person whose attitude is to be changed; the source is the person through whose influence the change happens.

Step 1: the target identifies with the source — the target likes and regards the source highly and puts herself or himself in the source's place. The source should also have a positive attitude towards the target.

Step 2: the source actually shows an attitude change by changing her or his own behaviour towards the attitude object. Observing this, the target imitates the source and changes her or his attitude and behaviour.

Characteristics of the existing attitude affect change: attitudes in a state of imbalance or dissonance are more open to change; extreme and central attitudes are harder to change than less extreme or peripheral ones; simple attitudes are easier to change than complex (multiplex) ones.

Direction of change: congruent change (same direction — a positive attitude becomes more positive) or incongruent change (opposite direction — a positive attitude becomes negative). An extreme attitude is especially hard to change incongruently.

ex.q: Neeraj admires his elder cousin, a doctor, who has always eaten fried snacks. The cousin starts eating fruits instead and talks about it. Neeraj soon does the same. Map this to Mohsin's steps.
st: Target: Neeraj; source: his doctor cousin.
Step 1: Neeraj identifies with and admires the cousin, who is also fond of him.
Step 2: the cousin changes his own behaviour (eating fruits); Neeraj observes and imitates.
ex.a: Step 1: identification with the source; Step 2: source shows the change, target imitates.

topics.rl: Public health campaigns in India often feature admired sportspersons who first adopt the behaviour themselves (e.g., getting vaccinated on camera), using Mohsin's second step.

rv.summary: Mohsin's two-step concept: the target first identifies with the source, then imitates the source's actual change in behaviour. Imbalanced, simple, peripheral and less extreme attitudes change more easily; change may be congruent or incongruent.

remember: Target: person whose attitude changes; source: person who influences
Step 1: identification; Step 2: source changes own behaviour, target imitates

traps: The target is not the person causing change
Central and extreme attitudes are hard, not easy, to change

topics.t: Source, message and target factors in attitude change
topics.h: Why do toothpaste ads show a dentist in a white coat? Who says it, what is said and who hears it all decide whether attitudes change.
p: Source characteristics: credibility (a highly credible, expert source produces more change) and attractiveness (an attractive or likeable source produces more change).

Message characteristics: the amount of information (attitudes change most when the information is just enough — neither too much nor too little); rational appeal (facts, e.g. 'saves fuel') versus emotional appeal (feelings, e.g. 'loving families choose this'); the motives the message activates (such as health, safety or status); and the mode of spreading (face-to-face messages are more effective than indirect ones like letters or pamphlets).

Target characteristics: persuasibility (people with open, flexible personalities change more easily); strong prejudices make change less likely; low self-esteem people change more easily than high self-esteem people; more intelligent people may change less easily, though sometimes they change more willingly because they base attitudes on more information and thinking.
Analysing an advertisement: identify the source (who), the appeal (rational or emotional), the motive activated, and the intended target audience.

ex.q: Analyse an ad: a famous cricketer smiles and says, 'Champions start their day with this cereal — be a champion!'
st: Source: attractive and popular, not necessarily an expert in nutrition.
Appeal: emotional — wanting to feel like a champion.
Motive activated: achievement and status.
Target: young sports fans.
ex.a: Attractive source, emotional appeal, achievement/status motive, young sports-fan audience.

topics.rl: Government health campaigns in India pair doctors (credibility) with film stars (attractiveness) and use both facts and emotions — covering all the bases of persuasion.

rv.summary: Attitude change depends on the source (credibility, attractiveness), the message (amount of information, rational or emotional appeal, motives, mode of spreading) and the target (persuasibility, prejudices, self-esteem, intelligence).
remember: Credibility: expert, trustworthy source; attractiveness: likeable source
Just-enough information changes attitudes most
Face-to-face is most effective
Low self-esteem → easier change
traps: A popular celebrity without expertise uses attractiveness, not credibility
Low self-esteem people lack, not have, confidence in their views
Too much information does not work best

topics.t: Attitude–behaviour relationship
topics.h: Almost everyone says littering is bad. Yet plastic bottles still pile up on beaches. Why don't our actions always match our attitudes?
p: Attitudes predict behaviour better when: the attitude is strong and occupies a central place in the attitude system; the person is aware of her or his attitude; there is very little or no external pressure to behave in a particular way.
Also when the person's behaviour is not being watched or evaluated by others, and when the person thinks the behaviour will have a positive consequence and so intends to engage in it.

LaPiere's study (1930s): LaPiere travelled across the USA with a Chinese couple and stayed in many hotels; they were refused service only once. Later, when hotel managers were sent a questionnaire asking whether they would accept Chinese guests, most said they would not — a gap between stated attitude and actual behaviour.

Behaviour can also shape attitudes. Festinger and Carlsmith asked students to do a very boring task and then tell others it was interesting. Students paid $1 for this later rated the task as more interesting than those paid $20 — with little external justification, they reduced dissonance by changing their attitude.

ex.q: Why did the $1 students, not the $20 students, change their attitude towards the boring task?
st: Both groups said the task was interesting, which conflicted with their experience.
$20 was enough external justification: 'I said it for the money.'
$1 was not enough justification, so dissonance remained.
They reduced it by believing the task really was interesting.
ex.a: Low payment gave too little justification, so they changed their attitude to reduce dissonance.

topics.rl: Many Indians support saving water in surveys, but behaviour improves most when households can see their own usage and there are positive consequences, like lower bills — matching the conditions for attitude–behaviour consistency.

rv.summary: Attitudes predict behaviour when strong and central, known to the person, under little external pressure or observation, and when a positive outcome is expected. LaPiere showed attitude–behaviour gaps; Festinger and Carlsmith showed behaviour can change attitudes.
remember: LaPiere: served almost everywhere, yet most managers said they would refuse Chinese guests
Festinger and Carlsmith: $1 group rated the boring task as more interesting
traps: The $20 group did not change its attitude; the $1 group did
Attitudes do not always predict behaviour
Being watched by others weakens, not strengthens, consistency

topics.t: Prejudice, stereotypes, discrimination and their sources
topics.h: 'People from that city are all rude.' One sentence — a stereotype, a prejudice and a possible seed of discrimination. Let's untangle them.
p: Prejudices are attitudes towards a particular group, usually negative and often based on stereotypes. A stereotype is a cluster of ideas about the characteristics of a group, assumed to be true of all its members; it is the cognitive component of prejudice and is often based on limited or incorrect information.
Discrimination is the behavioural component — negative actions towards members of a group. Prejudice can exist without discrimination, and discrimination can occur without prejudice.
Sources: learning — prejudices are learned through association, rewards and punishment, observation, group norms, family, reference groups, personal experiences and the media.

A strong social identity with an ingroup and ingroup bias can lead to negative attitudes towards outgroups. Scapegoating: a majority group blames a weaker minority outgroup for its own social, economic or political problems.

Kernel of truth: stereotypes may persist because there may be a small element of truth in them. Self-fulfilling prophecy: the target group behaves in ways that confirm the prejudice (e.g., a group labelled 'dull' loses motivation and performs poorly), keeping the prejudice alive.

ex.q: Label each: (a) 'All engineers are boring' (thought), (b) feeling dislike for engineers (feeling), (c) refusing to rent a flat to engineers (action).
st: (a) A generalised belief about a group = stereotype (cognitive).
(b) A negative feeling/attitude towards the group = prejudice.
(c) Negative action = discrimination (behavioural).
ex.a: (a) Stereotype, (b) Prejudice, (c) Discrimination.

topics.rl: The Indian Constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth (Article 15) — law tackles discriminatory behaviour, while education targets prejudiced attitudes.

rv.summary: Prejudice is a usually negative attitude towards a group; stereotypes are its cognitive part and discrimination its behavioural part. Sources include learning, strong social identity and ingroup bias, scapegoating, kernel of truth and self-fulfilling prophecy.
focus: Scapegoating, kernel of truth and self-fulfilling prophecy
remember: Stereotype: cognitive component
Discrimination: behavioural component
Scapegoating: majority blames a weaker minority
Self-fulfilling prophecy: target behaves in ways that confirm the prejudice
traps: Prejudice and discrimination can exist without each other
Ingroup bias favours one's own group
A stereotype is a belief, not an action

topics.t: Strategies for handling prejudice
topics.h: Put students from rival schools on one team for a national science fair. By the end, the 'rivals' are friends. Contact under the right conditions can melt prejudice.
p: Strategies are effective if they aim at: minimising opportunities for learning prejudices; changing negative attitudes; de-emphasising narrow social identity based on the ingroup; and discouraging the tendency towards self-fulfilling prophecy among victims of prejudice.
Education and information dissemination: correcting stereotypes about specific target groups and tackling strong ingroup bias.

Increasing intergroup contact (the contact hypothesis): direct communication removes mistrust and helps groups discover positive qualities in each other. It works best when the groups meet in a cooperative rather than competitive context, interact closely, and are not different in power or status.
Working towards shared, superordinate goals that neither group can achieve alone encourages cooperation and reduces ingroup–outgroup hostility.
Highlighting individual identity rather than group identity weakens the importance of group membership as a basis for judging others.

ex.q: A college finds tension between students from two hostels. Suggest two strategies based on psychology.
st: Create mixed teams for a project both hostels need to complete (cooperative contact with a superordinate goal).
Run information sessions correcting stereotypes each hostel holds about the other.
Encourage students to know each other as individuals, not just as 'Hostel A' or 'Hostel B'.
ex.a: Cooperative intergroup contact with shared goals, education to correct stereotypes, and emphasising individual identity.

topics.rl: India's school exchange programmes — students from different states living with host families — use the contact hypothesis to build understanding across regions and languages.

rv.summary: Prejudice is handled by limiting opportunities to learn it, changing negative attitudes, de-emphasising narrow ingroup identity and discouraging self-fulfilling prophecy. Methods: education, intergroup contact (under the right conditions), superordinate goals and stressing individual identity.
focus: The four aims of strategies against prejudice
remember: Contact hypothesis works with cooperative context, close interaction, similar status
Superordinate goal: achievable only by both groups together
Highlight individual identity over group identity
traps: Contact alone, in competition, can increase hostility
Superordinate does not mean one group above another
Keeping groups apart does not reduce prejudice

topics.t: What is a group? Features, and how groups differ from crowds, teams and audiences
topics.h: Forty people waiting at a bus stop and eleven players in the Indian cricket team — both are 'people together'. But only one is a true group. What's the difference?
p: Groups influence how we think and act. (In the rationalised syllabus this chapter covers the nature and formation of groups, types of groups, and group influences such as social loafing and group polarisation.)

A group is an organised system of two or more individuals who interact and are interdependent, have common motives, have set role relationships among members, and have norms that regulate members' behaviour.

Features: a social unit of two or more people who see themselves as belonging to the group; common motives and goals; interdependence (one member's actions affect others); members trying to satisfy needs through joint association and influencing each other; interaction governed by a set of norms; and defined roles.

A crowd is a collection of people present at a place by chance, with no structure, no feeling of belongingness and no interdependence; crowd behaviour can be irrational. An audience is a collection of people gathered for a special purpose, such as a film or a cricket match; it is generally passive, but may sometimes turn into a mob.

A team is a special kind of group whose members have complementary skills and are committed to a common goal, for which they hold themselves mutually accountable. In groups, performance depends on individual contributions; in teams, both individual contributions and teamwork matter, producing positive synergy.

ex.q: Classify: (a) people gathered after a minor road accident, (b) a school's quiz team with a history expert, a science expert and a sports expert, (c) viewers at a cinema hall.
st: (a) Gathered by chance, no structure → crowd.
(b) Complementary skills, common goal, mutual accountability → team.
(c) Gathered for a special purpose, mostly passive → audience.
ex.a: (a) Crowd, (b) Team, (c) Audience.

topics.rl: An ISRO mission team brings together engineers with complementary skills — propulsion, software, navigation — all accountable for one launch. That's a team, not just a group.

rv.summary: A group is an organised system of two or more interacting, interdependent people with common motives, roles and norms. A crowd is a chance gathering, an audience gathers for a purpose, and a team has complementary skills and mutual accountability.
focus: Definition and features of a group
Group vs crowd vs audience vs team
remember: Group: two or more people, interaction, interdependence, common motives, roles, norms
Crowd: chance, no structure
Audience: special purpose, passive
Team: complementary skills, mutual accountability, synergy
traps: A crowd is not a group: it has no structure or interdependence
People watching a match are an audience, not a team
A team needs complementary skills, not just people in one place

topics.t: Why people join groups and how groups form
topics.h: Why do you join a WhatsApp group of classmates, a dance club or a coaching batch? Each one fills a need — and some are formed simply because you sit close together.
p: Security: being in a group reduces insecurity and gives comfort and protection. Status: membership of a recognised group gives a feeling of importance, power and status.
Self-esteem: groups give feelings of self-worth and a positive social identity. Satisfaction of psychological and social needs: belongingness, giving and receiving attention, love and power.
Goal achievement: groups help achieve goals that cannot be achieved alone. Knowledge and information: groups provide information and widen our knowledge.

Group formation factors: proximity (repeated interaction with people nearby, such as classmates or neighbours), similarity (people like those with similar interests and attitudes; similarity also validates our views) and common motives and goals.

ex.q: Ananya joins her college's robotics club because (a) she wants to build a robot for a national contest, (b) club members are known as the 'tech elite' on campus, and (c) she can learn from seniors. Name the reasons.
st: (a) Achieving a goal not possible alone → goal achievement.
(b) Being part of a recognised, admired group → status.
(c) Learning from others → knowledge and information.
ex.a: (a) Goal achievement, (b) Status, (c) Knowledge and information.

topics.rl: Hostel friendships in Indian colleges often start simply because students live on the same floor — proximity at work.

rv.summary: People join groups for security, status, self-esteem, satisfaction of psychological and social needs, goal achievement and knowledge. Groups form through proximity, similarity and common motives and goals.
focus: The six reasons for joining groups
The three factors in group formation
Matching a case to the reason
remember: Reasons: security, status, self-esteem, psychological and social needs, goal achievement, knowledge and information
Formation: proximity, similarity, common motives and goals
traps: Similarity, not difference, attracts people into groups
Social loafing is not a reason for joining
Don't confuse status (importance) with self-esteem (self-worth)

topics.t: Stages of group formation and group structure
topics.h: A new project team: first awkward introductions, then arguments over who does what, then a rhythm sets in — and finally they deliver. Tuckman mapped this journey.
p: Bruce Tuckman's stages: Forming — uncertainty about the group, its goal and how to achieve it; members get to know each other; excitement and apprehension. Storming — intragroup conflict over how to achieve the goal, who controls the group and resources, and who does which task; at the end, a hierarchy of leadership develops.

Norming — members develop norms about group behaviour, leading to a positive group identity. Performing — the group's structure has evolved and is accepted, and the group works towards its goal (the final stage for some groups).

Adjourning — once the purpose is achieved, the group may be disbanded (e.g., a committee formed for a school function). Groups do not always move through the stages in a fixed order; they may go back and forth.

Group structure develops as members interact: roles (socially defined expectations people are expected to fulfil), norms (expected standards of behaviour and beliefs, agreed and enforced by members — the group's unwritten rules), status (the relative social position given to members; it may be ascribed, as through seniority, or achieved, through expertise or hard work) and cohesiveness (togetherness and mutual attraction among members — the 'we-feeling').

ex.q: Map a school annual-day committee to Tuckman's stages: (1) members meet and feel unsure, (2) they argue over who will host, (3) they agree on rules for rehearsals, (4) they put on the show, (5) the committee is dissolved.
st: (1) Forming
(2) Storming
(3) Norming
(4) Performing
(5) Adjourning
ex.a: Forming → Storming → Norming → Performing → Adjourning.

topics.rl: IPL franchise squads assembled through auctions go through forming and storming in pre-season camps; the best ones reach norming and performing quickly.

rv.summary: Tuckman's stages of group formation are forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning, though groups may move back and forth. Group structure includes roles, norms, status (ascribed or achieved) and cohesiveness.
focus: Order and features of Tuckman's five stages
The four elements of group structure
remember: Forming → storming → norming → performing → adjourning
Roles: expected behaviour; norms: unwritten rules; cohesiveness: 'we-feeling'
Achieved status: earned; ascribed status: e.g. seniority
traps: Storming (conflict) comes before norming
Achieved status is earned, not given by seniority
Stages are not always in a fixed order

topics.t: Types of groups
topics.h: Your family, your school's NCC unit, your lunch-break gang and the rival school's team. Each is a different type of group — and each affects you differently.
p: Primary groups are pre-existing formations usually given to the individual (such as the family). They involve face-to-face interaction, close physical proximity and warm emotional bonds, are central to individual functioning, shape values and ideals, and have less permeable boundaries.

Secondary groups are joined by choice (such as a professional association or a hobby club). Relationships are more impersonal, indirect and less frequent, and it is easy to leave and join another group.

Formal groups have explicitly stated functions, roles and rules (such as an office, a university or a school council). Informal groups form without specific rules, and members have close relationships (such as a group of friends).

Ingroup refers to one's own group ('we'); outgroup refers to another group ('they'). Ingroup members are seen as similar and are viewed favourably; outgroup members are often seen differently and less favourably.

Other collectivities include crowds (chance gatherings), audiences (gathered for a purpose, generally passive) and mobs (with a definite sense of purpose, polarised attention, homogeneity of thought and behaviour, and impulsivity).

ex.q: Classify the group types: (a) Rohit's family, (b) the Bar Council he joins as a lawyer, (c) his group of college friends, (d) his company's HR department.
st: (a) Given, warm, face-to-face → primary (and informal).
(b) Joined by choice, impersonal → secondary (and formal).
(c) No set rules, close bonds → informal.
(d) Explicit rules and roles → formal.
ex.a: (a) Primary, (b) Secondary/formal, (c) Informal, (d) Formal.

topics.rl: When two IPL franchises clash, fans strongly feel 'us' versus 'them' — a vivid example of ingroup and outgroup feelings, which is healthiest when the rivalry stays friendly and respectful.

rv.summary: Groups may be primary (given, warm, face-to-face) or secondary (chosen, impersonal), formal (stated rules and roles) or informal, and ingroups ('we') or outgroups ('they'). Other collectivities include crowds, audiences and mobs.
remember: Primary: family, warm bonds, shapes values
Secondary: joined by choice, impersonal
Formal: explicit rules and roles
Mob: definite purpose, polarised attention, homogeneity, impulsivity
traps: A professional association is secondary, not primary
Friends without rules form an informal, not formal, group
An audience is generally passive; a mob is impulsive

topics.t: Social facilitation and social loafing
topics.h: In tug-of-war, does each extra person pull as hard as they would alone? Experiments say no — and the reason has a name: social loafing.
p: Social facilitation: performance on well-learned or simple tasks improves in the presence of others (Norman Triplett found cyclists rode faster when racing with others than alone). The presence of others raises arousal; for new or complex tasks, performance may instead suffer.

Social loafing is a reduction in individual effort when working on a collective task, in which outputs are pooled with those of other members (e.g., tug-of-war). Latané and colleagues found people clapped and cheered less loudly per person in groups than alone.

Reasons: members feel less responsible for the overall task; motivation decreases because individual contributions are not evaluated; the group's performance is not compared with other groups; there is improper or no coordination; and belonging to the group is not important to members — it is only an aggregate of individuals. (Responsibility is spread or diffused across members.)

Reducing social loafing: make each person's effort identifiable; increase pressure to work hard by making members committed to successful performance; increase the apparent importance or value of the task; make people feel their individual contribution is important; and strengthen group cohesiveness.

ex.q: In a group project, only Riya does most of the work while others contribute little. Suggest two ways the teacher can reduce social loafing.
st: Assign each member a specific, named part so individual effort is identifiable.
Make the project important (e.g., a public presentation) and build cohesiveness so members care about the outcome.
ex.a: Make individual efforts identifiable and increase task importance and group cohesiveness.

topics.rl: In big office meetings in Indian companies, people often stay quiet expecting 'someone else will speak up'. Assigning named action points reduces that loafing.

rv.summary: Social facilitation is better performance on simple or well-learned tasks in others' presence (Triplett). Social loafing is reduced individual effort on pooled group tasks (Latané), caused by low responsibility and evaluation, and reduced by identifiability, importance and cohesiveness.
remember: Triplett: cyclists faster with others
Latané: less clapping per person in groups
Reduce loafing: identifiable effort, commitment, task importance, individual contribution, cohesiveness
traps: Others' presence does not always improve performance: complex new tasks may suffer
Cohesiveness reduces, not increases, loafing
Pooling outputs anonymously encourages loafing

topics.t: Group polarisation and groupthink
topics.h: Each member of a committee mildly favours a new flyover. After an hour of discussion, the group votes to build it immediately, whatever the cost. How did 'mild' become 'extreme'?
p: Group polarisation: groups are more likely to take extreme decisions than individuals alone; the group's initial position becomes stronger after discussion.

Reasons: (1) in the company of like-minded people, members hear new arguments favouring their own viewpoint; (2) when others share the same view, members feel their view is validated by the public — a bandwagon effect; (3) members perceive like-minded others as an ingroup, identify with the group and conform, so views become strengthened.

Groupthink (Irving Janis) is a related, extreme outcome of highly cohesive groups: the desire for consensus overrides realistic evaluation of alternatives. Signs include an illusion of unanimity, self-censorship of doubts and pressure on dissenters, often leading to poor decisions.
Preventing poor group decisions: encourage critical evaluation, invite outside opinions, and assign someone to play 'devil's advocate'.

ex.q: Before discussion, each member of a school council mildly supports banning phones on campus. After discussion they vote for a total ban with heavy fines. Explain using the reasons for group polarisation.
st: Members heard new arguments supporting the ban (more reasons to agree).
Seeing others agree validated their view (bandwagon effect).
Identifying with the like-minded group led them to conform and strengthen the position.
ex.a: Exposure to new supporting arguments, bandwagon validation and ingroup identification made the decision more extreme.

topics.rl: Social media echo chambers in India and elsewhere show group polarisation online: like-minded users share supporting posts, and views grow more extreme over time.

rv.summary: Group polarisation is the tendency of groups to make more extreme decisions than individuals, due to new supporting arguments, the bandwagon effect and ingroup identification. Groupthink (Janis) is the cohesive group's drive for consensus over realistic judgement.
focus: The three reasons for group polarisation
Ways to prevent poor group decisions
remember: Group polarisation: initial position becomes stronger after discussion
Bandwagon effect: view validated because others share it
Groupthink: Irving Janis; illusion of unanimity, self-censorship
traps: Polarisation pushes groups to extremes, not to the middle
Groupthink involves suppressing, not encouraging, dissent
Don't confuse group polarisation with social loafing

qa.q: Individual differences in psychology refer to:
qa.a: Distinctiveness and variations among people in characteristics and behaviour patterns
qa.e: Individual differences are the variations and distinctiveness among people in their characteristics and patterns of behaviour.

qa.q: Which of these is the best example of a trait?
qa.a: Meera is punctual in school, at tuition and with friends, year after year
qa.e: A trait is relatively stable and consistent across situations and time. Punctuality shown everywhere for years fits.

qa.q: The view that behaviour is largely shaped by situations and circumstances is called:
qa.e: Situationism holds that situations and circumstances strongly influence behaviour.

qa.q: A shy student speaks confidently at a family function but stays silent in a new class. This variation is best explained by:
qa.a: Interaction between the person and the situation
qa.e: The same person behaves differently in different contexts, showing that behaviour depends on person and situation together.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): People with very different personalities often behave alike at a solemn prayer meeting.
Reason (R): Strong situations carry clear expectations that can override individual trait differences.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion: the strong, rule-bound situation reduces trait-based differences.

qa.q: Why do psychologists study individual differences?
qa.a: To understand, describe and measure how and why people vary, so behaviour can be better understood and predicted
qa.e: Studying variations helps describe, measure and predict behaviour — for guidance, selection and support.

qa.q: Which statement about traits is correct?
qa.a: Traits are relatively stable, but behaviour also depends on situational demands
qa.e: Traits are fairly enduring, yet situations also shape what we actually do.

qa.q: Case: Two equally skilled shooters compete at a national event. One performs better in front of a large crowd, the other better in quiet practice. This mainly shows:
qa.a: Individual differences in how people respond to the same situation
qa.e: Equal skill but different reactions to the same crowd shows individual differences interacting with the situation.

qa.q: Formal assessment differs from informal assessment because formal assessment is:
qa.e: Formal assessment uses standardised, organised and objective procedures; informal assessment varies and is more subjective.

qa.q: Rohan has the potential to become a good pilot if trained. This refers to his:
qa.e: Aptitude is the underlying potential to acquire skills with training.

qa.q: 'Honesty is always the right way to live' — this enduring belief is an example of:
qa.e: Values are enduring beliefs about an ideal mode of behaviour.

qa.q: Which method gives an in-depth picture of one individual using data from many sources?
qa.e: A case study is an in-depth study of a person's psychological attributes and history, using interviews, observation and tests.

qa.q: A standardised and objective instrument for measuring an individual's mental or behavioural characteristics is called a:
qa.e: A psychological test is a standardised and objective measuring instrument.

qa.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
qa.a: Interest — preference for engaging in specific activities
qa.e: Interest is a preference for one or more specific activities. The other pairs are swapped.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Observation as a method requires systematic, organised and objective recording.
Reason (R): Casual watching without a plan gives reliable scientific data.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Scientific observation must be systematic and objective; casual unplanned watching is unreliable, so R is false.

qa.q: Case: A counsellor finds that Simran scores high on clerical aptitude but says she dislikes desk work. Her best prediction is that Simran:
qa.a: May not succeed fully in a clerical job, since success needs both aptitude and interest
qa.e: Aptitude and interest together predict success; high aptitude with low interest may not lead to satisfaction or success.

qa.q: According to Binet, intelligence is the ability to:
qa.a: Judge well, understand well and reason well
qa.e: Binet described intelligence in terms of good judgement, understanding and reasoning.

qa.q: Who defined intelligence as the global and aggregate capacity to think rationally, act purposefully and deal effectively with the environment?
qa.e: This is Wechsler's definition.

qa.q: The psychometric approach to intelligence treats intelligence as:
qa.a: An aggregate of abilities expressed as a single index and measured by tests
qa.e: The psychometric approach measures intelligence with tests and expresses it as a score.

qa.q: In Spearman's two-factor theory, 's' stands for:
qa.a: Specific factors unique to particular abilities
qa.e: Spearman proposed g (general) and s (specific) factors; s factors are unique to specific abilities.

qa.q: How many primary mental abilities did Thurstone propose?
qa.e: Thurstone listed seven primary mental abilities.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of Thurstone's primary mental abilities?
qa.e: Interpersonal intelligence belongs to Gardner's theory, not Thurstone's list.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Spearman believed that people who are good at one mental task tend to do reasonably well at others.
Reason (R): Spearman proposed a general factor g that underlies all mental tasks.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; the shared general factor g explains why performance across tasks tends to go together.

qa.q: Binet's theory is known as the uni-factor theory because it holds that:
qa.a: Intelligence consists of one similar set of abilities used for solving any problem
qa.e: Binet viewed intelligence as one general set of abilities.

qa.q: In Jensen's model, Level I abilities involve:
qa.a: Associative learning in which output is similar to input
qa.e: Level I is associative learning such as rote memory; output is similar to input.

qa.q: Solving a new reasoning problem by transforming given information is an example of Jensen's:
qa.e: Level II involves higher-order skills that transform the input.

qa.q: Guilford's structure-of-intellect model classifies abilities along which three dimensions?
qa.e: Guilford used operations, contents and products.

qa.q: How many intellectual abilities does Guilford's model propose?
qa.e: 6 operations × 5 contents × 6 products = 180.

qa.q: In Guilford's model, 'divergent production' belongs to which dimension?
qa.e: Divergent production is one of the six operations — what the person does.

qa.q: Which is one of Guilford's 'contents'?
qa.e: Contents are visual, auditory, symbolic, semantic and behavioural. Transformations and implications are products; evaluation is an operation.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Guilford's model contains 180 distinct abilities.
Reason (R): It combines 6 operations, 5 contents and 6 products, giving 6 × 5 × 6 cells.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; multiplying the three dimensions gives 180, which explains the count.

qa.q: Which comparison is correct?
qa.a: Spearman stressed a general factor; Guilford described many distinct abilities across three dimensions
qa.e: Spearman emphasised g plus s; Guilford proposed 180 abilities; Thurstone, not Jensen, proposed seven.

qa.q: Gardner's theory proposes that intelligence:
qa.a: Consists of distinct types that are relatively independent of each other
qa.e: Gardner proposed multiple, relatively independent intelligences.

qa.q: A sculptor who can rotate and manipulate shapes in her mind shows mainly:
qa.e: Spatial intelligence is forming, using and manipulating mental images.

qa.q: Which intelligence is most needed by a counsellor who must understand clients' feelings and motives?
qa.e: Interpersonal intelligence is understanding others' motives, feelings and behaviour.

qa.q: How many types of intelligence are described in Gardner's theory as taught in NCERT?
qa.e: Gardner's list in NCERT has eight: linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal and naturalistic.

qa.q: A spiritual leader known for deep insight into his own thoughts and emotions shows high:
qa.e: Intrapersonal intelligence is knowledge of one's own feelings, motives and desires.

qa.q: Case: Arjun, a national-level badminton player, can adjust his footwork in a split second during a rally. Which intelligence does this best show?
qa.e: Using the body with skill, flexibility and fine control is bodily-kinaesthetic intelligence.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): According to Gardner, a person highly gifted in music must also be highly gifted in logical-mathematical ability.
Reason (R): Gardner held that the different intelligences are relatively independent of each other.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: Gardner held that intelligences are relatively independent, so strength in one does not require strength in another. R is true.

qa.q: Which pairing is INCORRECT?
qa.e: Understanding others' motives is interpersonal; naturalistic is sensitivity to features of the natural world.

qa.q: Sternberg's triarchic theory proposes which three types of intelligence?
qa.e: Sternberg's three are componential (analytical), experiential (creative) and contextual (practical).

qa.q: A student plans how she will approach a difficult problem before starting. Which component of componential intelligence is this?
qa.e: Planning what to do and how to do it is the meta (higher-order) component.

qa.q: 'Street smartness' or 'business sense' corresponds to Sternberg's:
qa.e: Contextual intelligence deals with environmental demands in everyday life.

qa.q: Using past experience creatively to solve a brand-new problem reflects:
qa.e: Experiential (creative) intelligence uses past experiences creatively for novel problems.

qa.q: The PASS model was developed by:
qa.a: J.P. Das, Jack Naglieri and John Kirby
qa.e: Das, Naglieri and Kirby proposed the PASS model.

qa.q: Learning the spelling of 'psychology' letter by letter in order uses:
qa.e: Successive processing handles information serially, one item after another.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Planning is described as an essential feature of intelligence in the PASS model.
Reason (R): Planning lets a person decide a course of action, carry it out and evaluate its effectiveness.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; planning's role in setting, executing and checking actions is why it is considered essential.

qa.q: The Cognitive Assessment System (CAS) was designed to measure:
qa.a: The PASS processes of planning, attention-arousal, simultaneous and successive processing
qa.e: Das and Naglieri developed CAS as a battery of verbal and non-verbal tasks to assess PASS processes.

qa.q: A child has a mental age of 12 years and a chronological age of 10 years. What is the child's IQ?
A 12-year-old has a mental age of 9 years. Her IQ is:
An IQ of 75 falls in which NCERT category?
qa.e: 70–79 is the borderline range.

qa.q: Rahul is 8 years old and has an IQ of 125. What is his mental age?
The formula IQ = (MA ÷ CA) × 100 was introduced by:
qa.e: Binet gave the concept of mental age; William Stern devised the IQ ratio.

qa.q: Which statement about the distribution of IQ scores is correct?
qa.a: It is a symmetrical bell-shaped normal curve with mean 100
qa.e: IQ scores are normally distributed around a mean of 100; extreme scores are rare.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A child whose mental age equals her chronological age has an IQ of 100.
Reason (R): IQ is calculated as (CA ÷ MA) × 100.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: IQ = (MA ÷ CA) × 100, not CA ÷ MA.

qa.q: Case: Isha (CA 10 years) has an MA of 13 years. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: Her IQ is 130, in the superior range
qa.e: IQ = 13 ÷ 10 × 100 = 130. NCERT places 120–130 in 'superior'; 'very superior' is above 130.

qa.q: Which combination defines intellectual disability?
qa.a: Below-average intellectual functioning plus deficits in adaptive behaviour, appearing before 18
qa.e: The definition requires subaverage intellect, adaptive deficits and onset in the developmental period.

qa.q: Adaptive behaviour refers to:
qa.a: A person's ability to be self-reliant and adjust to the environment
qa.e: Adaptive behaviour covers self-care, communication, social and daily living skills.

qa.q: An IQ in the range of about 35–40 to 50–55 corresponds to:
qa.e: Moderate: about 35–40 to 50–55. Mild is about 55–70; severe is 20–25 to 35–40.

qa.q: People at which level of intellectual disability usually need constant care and support?
qa.e: Severe and profound levels involve the greatest need for continuous support.

qa.q: Giftedness differs from talent because giftedness is:
qa.a: Exceptional general ability shown across many areas
qa.e: Giftedness is broad; talent is remarkable ability in a specific field.

qa.q: Which is a recognised sign of a gifted child?
qa.e: Gifted children often think independently and are intrinsically motivated with fast processing.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A person with IQ 60 who shows no deficit in adaptive behaviour does not meet the definition of intellectual disability.
Reason (R): The definition of intellectual disability requires deficits in adaptive behaviour along with below-average intellect.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; because adaptive deficits are required, a low IQ alone is insufficient.

qa.q: Lewis Terman's well-known long-term study (1920s) followed:
qa.a: Children with high IQs to study how intelligence related to success and life adjustment
qa.e: Terman followed gifted, high-IQ children over many years.

qa.q: Which skills are typical of 'technological intelligence'?
qa.a: Generalisation, abstraction, speed and achievement orientation
qa.e: Technological intelligence values abstraction, speed, analysis and achievement.

qa.q: Integral intelligence emphasises:
qa.a: Connectivity with the social and natural environment
qa.e: Integral intelligence stresses relatedness with society and nature.

qa.q: Who described the Indian concept of 'buddhi' as including determination, will, conscience and self-knowledge along with cognition?
qa.e: J.P. Das described the broad Indian notion of buddhi.

qa.q: 'Respect for social order and commitment to elders, the young and the needy' belongs to which competency?
qa.e: These are listed under social competence in the Indian view.

qa.q: Commitment, persistence, patience and hard work make up:
qa.e: These goal-directed qualities form entrepreneurial competence.

qa.q: Sensitivity to context, discrimination, problem-solving and effective communication form:
qa.e: These are components of cognitive capacity in the Indian view.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): What counts as intelligent behaviour can differ between cultures.
Reason (R): Gardner proposed eight relatively independent types of intelligence.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but Gardner's list of intelligences does not explain why cultures differ in what they call intelligent; ideas like contextual intelligence and integral vs technological intelligence do.

qa.q: Case: In a village, Lakshmi is called 'very wise' because she settles disputes calmly, cares for neighbours and understands everyone's needs. This view of intelligence is closest to:
qa.e: Valuing harmony and social connectedness reflects integral intelligence.

qa.q: Who first introduced the concept of emotional intelligence?
qa.e: Salovey and Mayer introduced it; Goleman popularised it.

qa.q: According to Salovey and Mayer, emotional intelligence is the ability to:
qa.a: Monitor one's own and others' emotions, discriminate among them and use this to guide thinking and action
qa.e: That is their definition of EI.

qa.q: Which behaviour best shows empathy?
qa.a: Understanding and sharing a friend's feelings after she loses a match
qa.e: Empathy is understanding and feeling another person's emotions from their side.

qa.q: Reading a person's mood from tone of voice and facial expression is part of:
qa.a: Perceiving and detecting emotions in others
qa.e: Emotionally intelligent people detect emotions through body language, voice and expressions.

qa.q: Emotional literacy programmes in schools are intended to:
qa.e: These programmes build emotional skills, linked to better self-esteem and adjustment.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A person with a high IQ will always have a high EQ.
Reason (R): Emotional intelligence involves perceiving, understanding and regulating emotions, which is different from academic intelligence.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: high IQ does not guarantee high EQ. R is true: EI is a distinct set of emotional abilities.

qa.q: Case: Before replying to a rude comment in a group chat, Dev waits, calms down and then answers politely. He is showing:
qa.e: Controlling and regulating emotions before acting is a core EI feature.

qa.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of an emotionally intelligent person?
qa.a: Inability to notice changes in one's own feelings
qa.e: Emotionally intelligent people are aware of their own feelings; inability to notice them is the opposite.

qa.q: Aptitude is best described as:
qa.a: The potential to acquire specific knowledge or skills after training
qa.e: Aptitude refers to potential that can be developed with training.

qa.q: The Differential Aptitude Tests consist of how many subtests?
qa.e: The DAT has eight subtests.

qa.q: Who developed the Indian adaptation of the DAT mentioned in NCERT?
qa.e: J.M. Ojha adapted the DAT for Indian use.

qa.q: A test that measures only clerical aptitude is an example of:
qa.e: Independent aptitude tests measure one specific area.

qa.q: Which is NOT a DAT subtest?
qa.e: The DAT subtests are verbal, numerical, abstract reasoning, clerical speed and accuracy, mechanical reasoning, space relations, spelling and language usage.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A student with high aptitude for music but no interest in it may not do well as a musician.
Reason (R): Success in a field is better predicted by a combination of aptitude and interest.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; because success depends on aptitude plus interest, lack of interest can limit success.

qa.q: The main use of aptitude tests is to:
qa.a: Predict future performance to guide career choice and selection
qa.e: Aptitude tests predict how well a person can learn a skill, aiding guidance and selection.

qa.q: Case: An airline wants to choose trainees who will learn to fly quickly. What should it use?
qa.a: An aptitude test measuring relevant abilities like spatial and mechanical reasoning
qa.e: Aptitude tests predict the potential to learn a skill with training, which is what the airline needs.

qa.q: Creativity is the ability to produce ideas or products that are:
qa.e: Creative output must be new and also useful or appropriate.

qa.q: Creativity tests mainly assess:
qa.e: Creativity tests are open-ended and assess divergent thinking.

qa.q: In divergent thinking, 'flexibility' refers to:
qa.a: The variety of different categories or kinds of ideas
qa.e: Flexibility is variety; fluency is number; originality is unusualness; elaboration is detail.

qa.q: A student gives 20 uses of a spoon, but all are about eating. She scores high on:
qa.e: Many ideas = high fluency; all in one category = low flexibility.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A person with a very high IQ is always highly creative.
Reason (R): Beyond a certain level of intelligence, intelligence and creativity are only modestly related.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: high intelligence does not guarantee creativity. R is true: beyond a threshold the two are only modestly related.

qa.q: Which statement about the origins of creativity is correct?
qa.a: Heredity sets limits, but environment and opportunities strongly influence its development
qa.e: Both heredity and environment contribute; encouragement, freedom and opportunities matter greatly.

qa.q: Which of these shows creativity in the domain of science rather than art?
qa.a: Designing a low-cost water purifier from local materials
qa.e: Creativity varies by domain; a novel useful invention is scientific/technical creativity.

qa.q: How does an intelligence test item usually differ from a creativity test item?
qa.a: It has one correct answer, while a creativity item allows many answers
qa.e: Intelligence tests are largely convergent; creativity tests are divergent.

qa.q: Self is defined as:
qa.a: The totality of one's conscious experiences, ideas, thoughts and feelings about oneself
qa.e: The self is our conscious experiences, thoughts and feelings about ourselves.

qa.q: 'I am a member of the Indian Red Cross youth wing.' This statement reflects:
qa.e: Membership in a group is part of social identity.

qa.q: How does the self develop?
qa.a: Gradually, through interaction with family, friends, teachers and others
qa.e: Infants have no clear self; it develops through social interaction.

qa.q: When a person describes herself as 'I am a calm person', the self is acting as:
qa.e: The self that is observed and described is the self as object.

qa.q: A person whose self emphasises cooperation, unity, sacrifice and family ties has a strong:
qa.e: The social self values relationships and is also called the familial or relational self.

qa.q: Personality refers to:
qa.a: Our characteristic ways of responding to people and situations
qa.e: Personality is the characteristic, relatively consistent way a person responds across situations.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Personal identity refers to attributes that make a person different from others.
Reason (R): Social identity refers to aspects that link a person to a social or cultural group.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both statements are true definitions, but the definition of social identity does not explain what personal identity is.

qa.q: Case: Rohit says 'I want personal freedom and my own achievements matter most to me.' His orientation reflects:
qa.e: Concern with one's own freedom and achievements is the personal self.

qa.q: The value judgement a person makes about herself or himself is called:
qa.e: Self-esteem is the value we place on ourselves.

qa.q: The concept of self-efficacy is based on whose theory?
qa.e: Bandura introduced self-efficacy within social learning theory.

qa.q: A person with high self-efficacy is most likely to:
qa.a: Persist on a difficult task believing effort will succeed
qa.e: High self-efficacy means believing one can control outcomes, so one persists.

qa.q: By about what age do children start evaluating themselves in areas such as academic competence and physical appearance?
qa.e: By about 6–7 years, children form self-esteem judgements in several areas.

qa.q: 'I am good at painting but weak in sports.' This statement describes:
qa.e: Self-concept is how we perceive our competencies and attributes.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Children with high academic self-esteem tend to perform better in school.
Reason (R): Self-esteem has no relation with behaviour or performance.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Research links high academic self-esteem with better performance, so A is true and R is false.

qa.q: Which parenting style is linked with healthy self-esteem in children?
qa.e: Warm, positive parenting supports high self-esteem.

qa.q: Case: After watching her older cousin clear the NEET exam through steady study, Pooja starts believing she too can succeed if she works hard. This change is best explained by:
qa.a: Increase in self-efficacy through observing a model
qa.e: Watching a model succeed raises belief in one's own capability — self-efficacy via observational learning.

qa.q: Self-regulation refers to:
qa.a: Our ability to organise and monitor our own behaviour
qa.e: Self-regulation is the ability to monitor and control one's own behaviour.

qa.q: Learning to defer the satisfaction of a need is called:
qa.e: Delay of gratification means postponing satisfaction, a core self-control skill.

qa.q: A student rewards herself with her favourite snack after completing a chapter. This is:
qa.e: Rewarding oneself after desired behaviour is self-reinforcement.

qa.q: Which is an example of self-instruction?
qa.a: Telling yourself, 'First solve the easy questions, then the hard ones'
qa.e: Self-instruction means giving oneself directions about what to do.

qa.q: Fasting and non-attachment to worldly things are described in NCERT as:
qa.e: These traditional practices help develop control over desires.

qa.q: In the Indian view of self, the boundary between self and others is:
qa.e: The Indian view sees the self as able to include family and community; the Western view sees a firmer boundary.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Many Asian cultures, including India, are described as collectivistic.
Reason (R): In collectivistic cultures, group goals and relationships are given high importance.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; emphasis on group goals is exactly what makes a culture collectivistic.

qa.q: Case: Mehak wants to stop late-night snacking. Her counsellor first asks her to note down every time she snacks and what triggered it. Which technique is used first?
qa.e: Recording one's own behaviour provides the baseline for change — observation of own behaviour.

qa.q: The word 'personality' is derived from the Latin word 'persona', which means:
qa.e: Persona referred to the mask worn by actors in Roman theatre.

qa.q: Which is a characteristic of personality?
qa.a: Its main features are relatively stable, yet it is dynamic
qa.e: Personality is relatively stable and consistent but can change with demands.

qa.q: Hippocrates' typology classified people based on:
qa.e: Hippocrates proposed four types based on humours.

qa.q: The tridosha of Charak Samhita refers to:
qa.e: Charak Samhita classifies people by vata, pitta and kapha.

qa.q: A person showing envy, intense activity and a strong desire for material things is high on:
qa.e: Rajas involves activity, desire for sense gratification, envy and materialism.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): According to the triguna theory, every person has some sattva, rajas and tamas.
Reason (R): The tridosha of Charak Samhita consists of vata, pitta and kapha.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the tridosha is a different classification and does not explain the presence of the three gunas in everyone.

qa.q: Which of these is one of Hippocrates' four types?
qa.e: Hippocrates' types are sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric and melancholic.

qa.q: Why do psychologists study personality?
qa.a: To understand and predict how people are likely to behave across situations
qa.e: Personality helps explain and predict behaviour and supports guidance and selection.

qa.q: According to Sheldon, a person with a strong, muscular, rectangular body who is energetic and courageous is:
qa.e: Mesomorphs are muscular, energetic and courageous.

qa.q: Who classified people into introverts and extraverts?
qa.e: Jung's typology grouped people into introverts and extraverts. (Eysenck later used it as a trait dimension.)

qa.q: Type-A personality was described by:
qa.e: Friedman and Rosenman identified Type-A and Type-B.

qa.q: Type-A individuals are more susceptible to:
qa.e: Type-A traits are linked with hypertension and CHD.

qa.q: A person who is cooperative and unassertive, suppresses anger and complies with authority fits:
qa.e: Morris described Type-C this way and linked it to cancer.

qa.q: Someone who prefers being alone, avoids crowds and withdraws when emotionally upset is, in Jung's terms:
qa.e: Introverts prefer solitude and withdraw under emotional conflict.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Type approaches are often criticised as too simple.
Reason (R): Type approaches describe people on continuous dimensions rather than in categories.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: type approaches place people in discrete categories; trait approaches use continuous dimensions.

qa.q: How does a trait approach differ from a type approach?
qa.a: Traits describe people on continuous dimensions, whereas types place people in discrete categories
qa.e: Types sort people into categories; traits describe degrees along dimensions.

qa.q: Allport's 'cardinal traits' are:
qa.a: Highly generalised dispositions around which a person's entire life revolves
qa.e: Cardinal traits dominate a person's life, like Gandhi's non-violence.

qa.q: 'Likes to wear ethnic clothes' is an example of Allport's:
qa.e: Secondary traits are the least generalised preferences.

qa.q: Cattell's 16 PF is based on:
qa.a: Source traits identified through factor analysis
qa.e: Cattell used factor analysis to find source traits measured by the 16 PF.

qa.q: Eysenck's two original dimensions of personality were:
qa.a: Neuroticism vs emotional stability, and extraversion vs introversion
qa.e: Eysenck's first two dimensions; psychoticism vs sociability was added later.

qa.q: Who proposed the Five-Factor Model of personality?
qa.e: Costa and McCrae proposed the Big Five.

qa.q: A person who is anxious, moody, touchy and quickly loses control is high on:
qa.e: These features describe the neuroticism end of the dimension.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Surface traits in Cattell's theory are the result of interactions among source traits.
Reason (R): Cattell's 16 PF questionnaire is widely used with high school students, college students and adults.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the use of the 16 PF does not explain how surface traits arise from source traits.

qa.q: Case: Kunal is organised, punctual, responsible and works hard to achieve goals. On the Big Five he is high on:
qa.e: Achievement orientation, dependability and responsibility define conscientiousness.

qa.q: According to Freud, the id operates on the:
qa.e: The id seeks immediate gratification — the pleasure principle.

qa.q: The component often called the 'executive' of personality is the:
qa.e: The ego manages the demands of id, superego and reality.

qa.q: The superego develops mainly from:
qa.a: Internalisation of parental and social values
qa.e: The superego is the internalised moral standards learned from parents and society.

qa.q: Material you are not thinking about now but can easily recall, such as a friend's phone number, is in the:
qa.e: The preconscious holds information that can be brought to awareness with attention.

qa.q: The instinctual life force that energises the id is called:
qa.e: Libido is the life energy of the id; Thanatos is the death instinct.

qa.q: Which methods did Freud use to explore the unconscious?
qa.e: Freud used free association and interpretation of dreams.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The id works on the reality principle.
Reason (R): The id seeks immediate gratification without regard for morality, while the superego judges actions by moral standards.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the id works on the pleasure principle; the ego works on the reality principle. R is true.

qa.q: Case: Tanvi wants to skip school for a film (impulse), knows she will miss a test (reality), and feels guilty about lying to parents (morality). Her decision to watch the film on Sunday instead reflects the work of the:
qa.e: The ego finds a realistic way to satisfy the id without breaking moral or practical limits.

qa.q: According to Freud, defence mechanisms work by:
qa.e: Defence mechanisms protect the ego from anxiety through distortion of reality.

qa.q: Which defence mechanism did Freud consider the most common?
qa.e: Repression — pushing anxiety-provoking material into the unconscious — is the most common.

qa.q: A person with strong aggressive tendencies believes others are always hostile towards him. This is:
qa.e: Projection attributes one's own traits to others.

qa.q: A student who did poorly buys an expensive pen and says, 'With this pen I'll surely do better.' This is:
qa.e: Rationalisation makes unreasonable feelings or behaviour seem reasonable.

qa.q: In which stage do the Oedipus and Electra complexes occur?
qa.e: These complexes arise in the phallic stage, around 4–5 years.

qa.q: During which stage are the child's basic conflicts dormant while energy goes into social and school activities?
qa.e: The latency stage lasts from about seven years until puberty.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A 6-year-old starts bed-wetting again after the birth of a sibling.
Reason (R): Regression means returning to behaviour typical of an earlier stage under stress.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; the child's behaviour is an example of regression, which R defines.

qa.q: Fixation, in Freud's theory, means:
qa.a: Getting stuck at an earlier psychosexual stage due to an unresolved conflict
qa.e: Fixation is being stuck at a stage; regression is going back to one.

qa.q: Jung's 'collective unconscious' contains:
qa.a: Archetypes — primordial images shared by all humanity
qa.e: The collective unconscious holds archetypes common to all humans.

qa.q: Karen Horney explained psychological problems mainly in terms of:
qa.a: Disturbed interpersonal relationships in childhood causing basic anxiety
qa.e: Horney linked basic anxiety to parental indifference, discouragement and erratic behaviour.

qa.q: The concept of 'inferiority complex' is associated with:
qa.e: Adler proposed inferiority feelings and striving for superiority.

qa.q: Who described human beings as basically social beings who develop qualities like the desire for freedom and justice through relationships?
qa.e: This is Fromm's view.

qa.q: Erikson's theory places special emphasis on:
qa.a: Psychosocial development and the identity crisis of adolescence
qa.e: Erikson highlighted rational ego processes and the identity crisis.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Psychodynamic theories have been criticised for lacking a strong scientific base.
Reason (R): They were built largely on case studies, and many of their concepts are difficult to test.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; reliance on case studies and untestable concepts explains the criticism.

qa.q: Which is a criticism of Freud's theory?
qa.a: He used males as the prototype and neglected women's development
qa.e: Freud is criticised for sexist bias and small, atypical samples.

qa.q: Case: Raghav, short in height and teased as a child, works extremely hard and becomes a top athlete. Adler would explain this as:
qa.a: Striving for superiority to overcome feelings of inferiority
qa.e: Adler saw overcoming inferiority as a central motivating force.

qa.q: The core elements of the behavioural approach to personality are:
qa.e: Behaviourists view personality as learned responses: stimulus, response, reinforcement.

qa.q: According to the cultural approach, personality traits are:
qa.a: Adaptations to the ecology and culture of a group
